models.name: SevenNet-Nano
models.oneLiner: Knowledge-distilled lightweight universal MLIP inheriting SevenNet-Omni's generalization
models.description: SevenNet-Nano is a 2026 lightweight universal MLIP built on the SevenNet graph neural network architecture and produced by a knowledge-distillation framework rather than by direct training on raw DFT data. It inherits the broad generalization of SevenNet-Omni, a large multi-task foundation model trained across diverse materials datasets spanning chemical, configurational, and computational space, while being small enough for scalable atomistic simulation. It is representative of the dominant 2026 trend in the field — the frontier has shifted from 'train a bigger foundation model' to 'distill the foundation model into something you can actually run at scale', converging on the same efficiency niche NEP89 reached architecturally.
models.authors: SevenNet team (Seoul National University)
models.paperTitle: A Lightweight Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential via Knowledge Distillation for Scalable Atomistic Simulations

benchmarks.name: QM7
benchmarks.size: 7,165 molecules (up to 7 heavy atoms, CHNOS)
benchmarks.description: The original 'kernel-era' quantum chemistry ML benchmark, carved out of the GDB-13 enumeration. Introduced alongside the Coulomb matrix descriptor in Rupp et al.'s PRL, which is where ML-for-chemistry regression benchmarking effectively begins. Single equilibrium geometry per molecule, one target (atomization energy), so it is a pure property-regression set with no forces. Long since saturated and superseded by QM9, but still cited as the field's origin point.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Fast and Accurate Modeling of Molecular Atomization Energies with Machine Learning
benchmarks.creators: Matthias Rupp, Alexandre Tkatchenko, Klaus-Robert Müller, O. Anatole von Lilienfeld

sota.note: Later kernel/NN methods pushed this below 1 kcal/mol; benchmark is considered saturated.

benchmarks.name: QM7b
benchmarks.size: 7,211 molecules (CHNOSCl)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Multiple: PBE0, ZINDO, SCS, GW (14 electronic properties)
benchmarks.description: Extension of QM7 to multiple electronic properties per molecule (atomization energies, polarizability, HOMO/LUMO, excitation energies, ionization potential, electron affinity) computed at several levels of theory. Introduced in the context of multi-task deep learning across chemical space. Notable as the first widely used multi-property small-molecule benchmark, and the direct conceptual ancestor of QM9's 12-target setup.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Machine learning of molecular electronic properties in chemical compound space
benchmarks.creators: Grégoire Montavon, Matthias Rupp, Vivekanand Gobre, Alvaro Vazquez-Mayagoitia, Katja Hansen, Alexandre Tkatchenko, Klaus-Robert Müller, O. Anatole von Lilienfeld

benchmarks.name: QM8
benchmarks.size: ~21,800 molecules (up to 8 heavy atoms)
benchmarks.description: The excited-state counterpart to QM9, built on the smaller GDB-8 subset. Provides the two lowest singlet vertical excitation energies and oscillator strengths from TD-DFT and CC2. Its distinguishing feature is Δ-learning: the paper trains ML on the CC2−TDDFT difference rather than absolute values. Remains one of the very few standard benchmarks targeting excited states rather than ground-state energies/forces, and is part of MoleculeNet.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Electronic Spectra from TDDFT and Machine Learning in Chemical Space
benchmarks.creators: Raghunathan Ramakrishnan, Mia Hartmann, Enrico Tapavicza, O. Anatole von Lilienfeld

benchmarks.name: QM9
benchmarks.size: 133,885 molecules (up to 9 heavy atoms: C, N, O, F)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: B3LYP/6-31G(2df,p) (geometries + 12 properties); G4MP2 for a later subset
tasks: scalar property regression (U0, HOMO, LUMO, gap, dipole, polarizability, ZPVE, Cv, …)
benchmarks.description: By far the most-used molecular property benchmark in ML, and the de facto MNIST of quantum chemistry. 134k GDB-17-derived molecules with relaxed B3LYP geometries and 12-13 thermochemical/electronic targets. Its ubiquity is also its weakness: it has a single conformer per molecule, no forces, and B3LYP-level accuracy, so it measures interpolation over a narrow chemical space and is widely regarded as saturated (top models are below DFT's own error vs. experiment). Still the standard sanity check for any new equivariant GNN architecture.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Quantum chemistry structures and properties of 134 kilo molecules
benchmarks.creators: Raghunathan Ramakrishnan, Pavlo O. Dral, Matthias Rupp, O. Anatole von Lilienfeld
institutions: Max Planck Institute for Coal Research

sota.model: Various equivariant GNNs (e.g. ViSNet, Equiformer-class, MACE)
sota.note: Leading models cluster in the 5-7 meV range on U0; differences are within noise of the split and the benchmark is broadly considered saturated. Exact per-model values vary by split and training budget — verify against the specific paper.
Historical reference point.
Historical reference point.

benchmarks.name: QM9-G4MP2
benchmarks.size: ~133k molecules (G4MP2 for the full set; earlier subsets ~30k)
benchmarks.description: A higher-fidelity relabeling of QM9 at the G4MP2 composite level, which is roughly an order of magnitude more accurate than B3LYP for formation enthalpies. Its main research use is multi-fidelity and Δ-learning: train on abundant cheap B3LYP data and correct to sparse expensive G4MP2 labels. Directly addresses the criticism that QM9's B3LYP labels cap achievable accuracy.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Accurate and transferable machine learning models of formation enthalpies from limited chemical accuracy data
benchmarks.creators: Bhaskar Narayanan, Peter C. Redfern, Rajeev S. Assary, Larry A. Curtiss (and related work by Logan Ward et al.)

benchmarks.name: QM7-X
benchmarks.size: ~4.2 million equilibrium and non-equilibrium structures from 6,950 molecules (up to 7 heavy atoms)
benchmarks.description: A deliberate answer to QM9's single-conformer limitation: QM7-X samples constitutional and conformational isomers plus non-equilibrium distortions, giving ~4.2M structures with 42 properties each at PBE0+MBD (which includes many-body dispersion, unlike most datasets). Provides forces, so it can train interatomic potentials rather than only property regressors. Especially useful for testing whether models learn physics or memorize equilibrium geometries.
benchmarks.paperTitle: QM7-X: A comprehensive dataset of quantum-mechanical properties spanning the chemical space of small organic molecules
benchmarks.creators: Johannes Hoja, Leonardo Medrano Sandonas, Brian G. Ernst, Alvaro Vazquez-Mayagoitia, Robert A. DiStasio Jr., Alexandre Tkatchenko

benchmarks.name: ANI-1 dataset
benchmarks.size: ~20 million off-equilibrium conformations from 57,462 molecules (CHNO, up to 8 heavy atoms)
benchmarks.description: The dataset that made transferable neural network potentials credible. Rather than one geometry per molecule, it normal-mode-samples ~20M off-equilibrium conformations from 57k GDB-11 molecules, which is what lets a model trained on it generalize to molecules far larger than those it saw. Energies only (no forces in the original release). The direct ancestor of the ANI-1x/ANI-1ccx/ANI-2x line and of essentially every later 'foundation model' molecular dataset.
benchmarks.paperTitle: ANI-1, A data set of 20 million calculated off-equilibrium conformations for organic molecules
benchmarks.creators: Justin S. Smith, Olexandr Isayev, Adrian E. Roitberg
institutions: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

benchmarks.name: ANI-1x
benchmarks.size: ~5 million conformations (CHNO)
benchmarks.description: Built by active learning rather than exhaustive sampling: ~5M conformations selected because a model ensemble was uncertain about them, which makes it far more information-dense per point than ANI-1's 20M. Includes forces and multiple property sets. Released jointly with ANI-1ccx and now one of the most common pretraining corpora for transfer-learning to coupled-cluster accuracy.
benchmarks.paperTitle: The ANI-1ccx and ANI-1x data sets, coupled-cluster and density functional theory properties for molecules
benchmarks.creators: Justin S. Smith, Roman Zubatyuk, Benjamin Nebgen, Nicholas Lubbers, Kipton Barros, Adrian E. Roitberg, Olexandr Isayev, Sergei Tretiak

benchmarks.name: ANI-1ccx
benchmarks.size: ~500,000 conformations (CHNO)
benchmarks.description: The coupled-cluster companion to ANI-1x: ~500k conformations relabeled at CCSD(T)*/CBS, the highest level of theory available at this scale. Its canonical use is the two-stage recipe of pretraining on ANI-1x DFT data then fine-tuning on ANI-1ccx, which was shown to beat DFT-trained models against experiment. Small by modern standards, but still one of the only large CCSD(T) force-field corpora in existence.
benchmarks.paperTitle: The ANI-1ccx and ANI-1x data sets, coupled-cluster and density functional theory properties for molecules
benchmarks.creators: Justin S. Smith, Roman Zubatyuk, Benjamin Nebgen, Nicholas Lubbers, Kipton Barros, Adrian E. Roitberg, Olexandr Isayev, Sergei Tretiak

sota.value: chemical accuracy (~1 kcal/mol) on benchmark reactions
sota.note: Reported in the Smith et al. 'Approaching coupled cluster accuracy with a general-purpose neural network potential through transfer learning' Nature Communications paper.

benchmarks.name: ANI-2x dataset
benchmarks.size: ~8.9 million conformations, 7 elements (H, C, N, O, F, Cl, S)
benchmarks.description: Extends the ANI line beyond CHNO to sulfur and halogens (F, Cl), which is what made ANI usable for real medicinal chemistry — the CHNO-only restriction had excluded a large fraction of drug molecules. Built with the same active-learning machinery as ANI-1x. The ANI-2x model trained on it became a widely deployed general-purpose organic NNP.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Extending the Applicability of the ANI Deep Learning Molecular Potential to Sulfur and Halogens
benchmarks.creators: Christian Devereux, Justin S. Smith, Kate K. Davis, Kipton Barros, Roman Zubatyuk, Olexandr Isayev, Adrian E. Roitberg

benchmarks.name: MD17
benchmarks.size: ~100k-1M MD frames per molecule, 10 small organic molecules (benzene, aspirin, ethanol, malonaldehyde, naphthalene, salicylic acid, toluene, uracil, paracetamol, azobenzene)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: PBE+vdW-TS (original DFT); a CCSD(T)/CCSD subset also exists for 5 molecules
benchmarks.description: The canonical force-field benchmark: AIMD trajectories for a handful of small molecules, where the task is to fit a potential for one molecule at a time from few samples. Introduced with sGDML. Its enormous influence is matched by a well-known flaw — the reference DFT energies/forces are numerically noisy relative to the accuracy models now reach, so sub-noise MAEs on MD17 are not meaningful. This is precisely what motivated rMD17.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Machine Learning of Accurate Energy-Conserving Molecular Force Fields
benchmarks.creators: Stefan Chmiela, Alexandre Tkatchenko, Huziel E. Sauceda, Igor Poltavsky, Kristof T. Schütt, Klaus-Robert Müller

sota.note: Original paper's headline result; ~0.3 kcal/mol for energies.

benchmarks.name: revised MD17 (rMD17)
benchmarks.size: 100,000 structures per molecule, 10 molecules (same set as MD17)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: PBE/def2-SVP with very tight SCF and dense grids (recomputed to remove numerical noise)
tasks: few-shot force field fitting (standard splits: 50/100/200/400/800/1000 train)
benchmarks.description: A recomputation of MD17 with tight convergence settings, created because the original MD17 labels carried numerical noise larger than the errors modern MLIPs claim. Ships standard train/test index splits, which made cross-paper comparison meaningful for the first time. rMD17 — not MD17 — is now the correct choice for benchmarking, and is the set MACE, NequIP, Allegro and successors report on.
benchmarks.paperTitle: On the role of gradients for machine learning of molecular energies and forces
benchmarks.creators: Anders S. Christensen, O. Anatole von Lilienfeld

sota.note: MACE reported state-of-the-art on rMD17 at release; exact per-molecule numbers are in Table 1 of arXiv:2206.07697. Several later models (Allegro, BOTNet, equivariant transformers) report comparable values — differences are often within reference-data noise.
Established the E(3)-equivariant, data-efficient regime on this benchmark.

benchmarks.name: MD22
benchmarks.size: 7 large systems, 42-370 atoms, ~5k-100k frames each (Ac-Ala3-NHMe, DHA, stachyose, AT-AT, AT-AT-CG-CG, buckyball catcher, double-walled nanotube)
tasks: energy and force prediction at scale
benchmarks.description: The explicit successor to MD17, designed to break models that only ever saw <20-atom molecules. Spans peptides, a lipid, a carbohydrate, DNA base pairs, and two supramolecular complexes up to 370 atoms, with PBE+MBD labels that include many-body dispersion. The buckyball catcher and nanotube systems specifically stress long-range/non-local interactions, which is where strictly local message-passing models tend to fail.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Accurate global machine learning force fields for molecules with hundreds of atoms
benchmarks.creators: Stefan Chmiela, Valentin Vassilev-Galindo, Oliver T. Unke, Adil Kabylda, Huziel E. Sauceda, Alexandre Tkatchenko, Klaus-Robert Müller

sota.note: Original paper baseline.

sota.model: Equivariant GNNs with long-range corrections (e.g. Neural P3M, ViSNet-LSRM)
sota.value: improved over local-only baselines on buckyball catcher / DWNT
sota.note: Long-range systems are the discriminating subset; see arXiv:2409.17622 and arXiv:2304.13542.

benchmarks.name: 3BPA
benchmarks.size: 3-(benzyloxy)pyridin-2-amine; ~500 training frames at 300 K, test sets at 300/600/1200 K plus dihedral scans
benchmarks.description: A small but unusually diagnostic benchmark: train on 300 K frames, test at 600 K and 1200 K. It measures extrapolation to unseen regions of the PES rather than interpolation, which is the failure mode that actually matters for MD stability. Introduced in the 'beyond RMSE' paper, whose thesis is that aggregate force MAE hides qualitative PES errors — the 2D dihedral scans expose these directly. Now a standard reporting target for MACE-class models.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Linear Atomic Cluster Expansion Force Fields for Organic Molecules: Beyond RMSE
benchmarks.creators: Dávid Péter Kovács, Cas van der Oord, Jiri Kucera, Alice E. A. Allen, Daniel J. Cole, Christoph Ortner, Gábor Csányi

sota.note: MACE reported reaching/exceeding SOTA on 3BPA; the 1200 K split is the hard one. See arXiv:2206.07697 for the table.

benchmarks.name: AcAc (acetylacetone)
benchmarks.size: Acetylacetone; training at 300 K, test at 300/600 K plus proton-transfer and dihedral scans
benchmarks.description: Companion benchmark to 3BPA from the same 'beyond RMSE' paper. Acetylacetone's intramolecular proton transfer gives a genuine reactive barrier, so the test is whether a model reproduces a chemically meaningful transition rather than just low average force error. Like 3BPA, it uses train-cold/test-hot splits. Small, cheap, and a good early smoke test for reactive PES quality.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Linear Atomic Cluster Expansion Force Fields for Organic Molecules: Beyond RMSE
benchmarks.creators: Dávid Péter Kovács, Cas van der Oord, Jiri Kucera, Alice E. A. Allen, Daniel J. Cole, Christoph Ortner, Gábor Csányi

benchmarks.name: SPICE (Small-Molecule/Protein Interaction Chemical Energies)
benchmarks.size: SPICE 2.0: 113,999 molecules/clusters, 2,008,628 conformations, 2-110 atoms, 17 elements (H, Li, B, C, N, O, F, Na, Mg, Si, P, S, Cl, K, Ca, Br, I)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: wB97M-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVPPD (Psi4), with DFT-D3 dispersion; includes energies, forces, and additional properties (MBIS charges, dipoles, quadrupoles, bond orders)
benchmarks.domain: biomolecules / drug-like molecules, peptides, protein-ligand interaction energies
tasks: Energy and force regression on drug-like molecules, dipeptides, solvated amino acids, PubChem molecules, ion pairs, water clusters
Charge/multipole prediction (MBIS partial charges, dipoles, quadrupoles)
Transferability evaluation: small-molecule-trained models applied to peptides and protein environments
benchmarks.description: SPICE is the dataset that made general-purpose biomolecular MLIPs possible. Its design solves the specific problem that earlier QM datasets (QM9, ANI-1x) covered small neutral organics but not the charged, ion-containing, peptide-and-drug chemical space that biomolecular simulation actually needs. It deliberately samples dimers, ion pairs, and solvated amino acids alongside PubChem drug-like molecules, at a level of theory (wB97M-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVPPD) chosen for accuracy on noncovalent interactions. It is the training set behind MACE-OFF, Nutmeg, AIMNet2, and Espaloma-family models. CC0 licensing has been a significant factor in its adoption.
benchmarks.paperTitle: SPICE, A Dataset of Drug-like Molecules and Peptides for Training Machine Learning Potentials
benchmarks.creators: Peter Eastman, Pavan Kumar Behara, David L. Dotson, Raimondas Galvelis, John E. Herr, Josh T. Horton, Yuezhi Mao, John D. Chodera, Benjamin P. Pritchard, Yuanqing Wang, Gianni De Fabritiis, Thomas E. Markland

sota.metric: SPICE test set force MAE (meV/A) and energy MAE (meV)
sota.note: MACE-OFF is the flagship SPICE-trained organic/biomolecular foundation potential (Kovacs, Batatia, Csanyi et al.). Verify exact MAEs from the paper.

sota.metric: SPICE 2.0 energy/force accuracy with explicit charge conditioning
sota.note: Eastman et al., J. Chem. Theory Comput. 20(19), 8583-8593 (2024) — 'Nutmeg and SPICE: Models and Data for Biomolecular Machine Learning'. Introduced alongside SPICE 2.0.

sota.metric: SPICE-family energy/force accuracy incl. charged species
sota.note: Notable for handling charge and long-range electrostatics explicitly.

benchmarks.name: SPICE-2
benchmarks.size: ~2 million conformations, ~114,000 molecules/clusters, 17 elements
benchmarks.description: Major expansion of SPICE (roughly 2x conformations, ~6x molecules, 17 elements), released alongside the Nutmeg models. Broadens chemical coverage where SPICE-1-trained models were found weakest, notably in underrepresented element/functional-group combinations. Version 2.0.1 (April 2024) is the current release. CC0-licensed, which is part of why it has become the community default.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Nutmeg and SPICE: Models and Data for Biomolecular Machine Learning
benchmarks.creators: Peter Eastman, Benjamin P. Pritchard, John D. Chodera, Thomas E. Markland

benchmarks.name: Nutmeg (models + data)
benchmarks.size: Models trained on SPICE-2 (~2M conformations); small/medium/large variants
benchmarks.description: A set of transferable biomolecular potentials released with SPICE-2. Its notable design choice is conditioning on precomputed partial charges as an input feature, which gives the model a route to total-charge and long-range electrostatic awareness that pure local NNPs lack — a direct response to the known failure of MLIPs on charged species. Serves as the reference baseline on SPICE-2.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Nutmeg and SPICE: Models and Data for Biomolecular Machine Learning
benchmarks.creators: Peter Eastman, Benjamin P. Pritchard, John D. Chodera, Thomas E. Markland

sota.metric: force and energy MAE on SPICE-2 test
sota.value: baseline reference values reported in the paper
sota.note: Published as the reference baseline for SPICE-2; see JCTC 10.1021/acs.jctc.4c00794.

benchmarks.name: GEOM / GEOM-Drugs
benchmarks.size: ~37 million conformations for ~450,000 molecules (GEOM-Drugs: ~304k drug-like molecules; GEOM-QM9 subset also provided)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: GFN2-xTB (semi-empirical), with CREST conformer search; energies annotated
benchmarks.description: The standard benchmark for 3D molecular conformer generation and 3D generative models. Uses CREST + GFN2-xTB to produce energy-annotated conformer ensembles with Boltzmann weights, trading DFT accuracy for the scale needed to cover conformational space. GEOM-Drugs in particular is what diffusion/flow-matching conformer models are evaluated on. Note the semi-empirical level: it is a geometry/ensemble benchmark, not an energy-accuracy benchmark.
benchmarks.paperTitle: GEOM: Energy-annotated molecular conformations for property prediction and molecular generation
benchmarks.creators: Simon Axelrod, Rafael Gómez-Bombarelli

sota.model: Diffusion / flow-matching conformer generators (e.g. torsional diffusion and successors)
sota.note: Active benchmark; see arXiv:2506.15378 and arXiv:2510.04878 for recent entries. Numbers are highly protocol-dependent — cite from the specific paper.

benchmarks.name: PubChemQC (PM6 / B3LYP)
benchmarks.size: PubChemQC PM6: ~221 million molecules; PubChemQC B3LYP/6-31G*//PM6: ~86 million molecules; original project ~3M excited-state calcs
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: PM6 (geometries); B3LYP/6-31G* single-points on PM6 geometries; TD-DFT for excited states
benchmarks.description: The largest-by-molecule-count quantum chemistry database, derived from PubChem. Released in escalating tiers: the original project, then PM6 geometries for 221M molecules, then B3LYP/6-31G* electronic structures for 86M. Its value is scale and chemical breadth for pretraining; the tradeoff is that geometries are semi-empirical (PM6) and there are no forces, so it is a property/pretraining corpus rather than an MLIP training set.
benchmarks.paperTitle: PubChemQC B3LYP/6-31G*//PM6 dataset: the Electronic Structures of 86 Million Molecules using B3LYP/6-31G* calculations
benchmarks.creators: Maho Nakata, Toshiyuki Maeda, Tomomi Shimazaki, Masatomo Hashimoto

sota.note: Primarily a pretraining corpus; see also the original project (arXiv:1512.08572) and PubChemQC PM6 (arXiv:1904.06046). A relaxation benchmark built on it appeared in 2025 (arXiv:2506.23008).

benchmarks.name: Alchemy
benchmarks.size: ~119,000 organic molecules (up to 14 heavy atoms, C/N/O/F/S/Cl)
benchmarks.description: A deliberate QM9 extension: same 12 property targets and same level of theory, but molecules up to 14 heavy atoms and a wider element set (adds S, Cl). Designed so models can be trained on small molecules and tested on larger ones, probing size extrapolation — the specific weakness QM9's fixed ≤9-heavy-atom cap cannot test. Released with a competition/leaderboard.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Alchemy: A Quantum Chemistry Dataset for Benchmarking AI Models
benchmarks.creators: Guangyong Chen, Pengfei Chen, Chang-Yu Hsieh, Chee-Kong Lee, Benben Liao, Renjie Liao, Weiwen Liu, Jiezhong Qiu, Qiming Sun, Jie Tang, Richard Zemel, Shengyu Zhang

benchmarks.name: Molecule3D
benchmarks.size: ~3.9 million molecules with ground-state 3D geometries
benchmarks.description: Reframes the task: instead of predicting properties from a given 3D structure, predict the DFT ground-state geometry itself from the 2D graph. Curated from PubChemQC at ~3.9M molecules with defined random and scaffold splits. Fills a real gap, since at inference time DFT geometries are exactly what you do not have — making this a test of whether 3D-dependent property models are usable in practice.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Molecule3D: A Benchmark for Predicting 3D Geometries from Molecular Graphs
benchmarks.creators: Zhao Xu, Youzhi Luo, Xuan Zhang, Xinyi Xu, Yaochen Xie, Meng Liu, Kaleb Dickerson, Cheng Deng, Maho Nakata, Shuiwang Ji

benchmarks.name: OrbNet-Denali dataset
benchmarks.size: ~2.3 million conformers from ~215,000 molecules and complexes
benchmarks.domain: drug-like and biological molecules, including charged species and protonation states
benchmarks.description: Training set for the OrbNet Denali model, covering neutral and charged drug-like molecules, protonation/tautomer states, non-covalent complexes and transition-metal-free biological chemistry. Distinctive for its emphasis on charge states and its use of symmetry-adapted atomic-orbital features rather than raw geometry — OrbNet learns a correction on top of a cheap GFN semi-empirical calculation, achieving DFT accuracy at semi-empirical cost.
benchmarks.paperTitle: OrbNet Denali: A machine learning potential for biological and organic chemistry with semi-empirical cost and DFT accuracy
benchmarks.creators: Anders S. Christensen, Sai Krishna Sirumalla, Zhuoran Qiao, Michael B. O'Connor, Daniel G. A. Smith, Feizhi Ding, Peter J. Bygrave, Animashree Anandkumar, Matthew Welborn, Frederick R. Manby, Thomas F. Miller III

sota.note: Headline claim of the original paper.

benchmarks.name: Transition1x
benchmarks.size: ~9.6 million DFT calculations along ~10,000 reaction pathways
benchmarks.description: Fills a conspicuous gap: nearly every MLIP dataset samples near-equilibrium geometries, so models trained on them are unreliable exactly at transition states. Transition1x harvests intermediate geometries from NEB calculations on ~10k reactions, deliberately concentrating data on and around barriers. Essential for reactive MLIPs, and commonly paired with RGD1 and the T1x-derived evaluations.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Transition1x — a Dataset for Building Generalizable Reactive Machine Learning Potentials
benchmarks.creators: Mathias Schreiner, Arghya Bhowmik, Tejs Vegge, Jonas Busk, Ole Winther

sota.note: The paper's key finding is that models trained only on near-equilibrium data (e.g. ANI-1x) fail badly on barrier regions, while Transition1x-trained models do not.

benchmarks.name: RGD1 (Reaction Graph Depth 1)
benchmarks.size: ~176,000 organic reactions with ~1.3 million geometries; reactants, products and transition states
benchmarks.description: A large, systematically enumerated reaction dataset built by graph-based exploration of elementary (depth-1) reaction space rather than by harvesting literature reactions, which avoids the reporting bias of experimental corpora. Provides located transition states with verified intrinsic reaction coordinates. Complements Transition1x and is a standard target for generative TS-prediction models.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Comprehensive exploration of graphically defined reaction spaces
benchmarks.creators: Qiyuan Zhao, Sai Mahit Vaddadi, Michael Woulfe, Lawal A. Ogunfowora, Sanjay S. Garimella, Olexandr Isayev, Brett M. Savoie

benchmarks.name: DES370K / DES5M
benchmarks.size: DES370K: ~370,000 dimer geometries (~3,700 dimers); DES5M: ~5 million dimer geometries
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: DES370K: CCSD(T)/CBS ('gold standard'); DES5M: SNS-MP2 ('silver standard')
benchmarks.description: The largest gold-standard CCSD(T)/CBS dimer interaction-energy database, with SAPT energy decompositions (electrostatics, exchange, induction, dispersion) rather than just total energies — which lets you diagnose *which* physical component a model gets wrong. DES5M extends the same chemistry to 5M geometries at a cheaper level. Widely used to test whether MLIPs capture non-covalent physics, and DES370K is incorporated as a SPICE subset.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Quantum chemical benchmark databases of gold-standard dimer interaction energies
benchmarks.creators: Alexander G. Donchev, Andrew G. Taube, Elizabeth Decolvenaere, Cory Hargus, Robert T. McGibbon, Ka-Hei Law, Brent A. Gregersen, Je-Luen Li, Kim Palmo, Karthik Siva, Michael Bergdorf, John L. Klepeis, David E. Shaw

benchmarks.name: nablaDFT / ∇²DFT
benchmarks.size: ∇²DFT: ~2 million conformations from ~1 million drug-like molecules, with Hamiltonian matrices
benchmarks.description: Unusual in providing the full Hamiltonian, overlap and core-Hamiltonian matrices alongside energies — enabling models that predict the electronic structure rather than only its scalar outputs, which is a fundamentally different and more transferable target. ∇²DFT (2024) expands the original ∇DFT (2023) and adds a structured benchmark suite spanning property prediction, Hamiltonian prediction and relaxation, with leaderboard-style baselines.
benchmarks.paperTitle: ∇²DFT: A Universal Quantum Chemistry Dataset of Drug-Like Molecules and a Benchmark for Neural Network Potentials
benchmarks.creators: Kuzma Khrabrov, Anton Ber, Artem Tsypin, Konstantin Ushenin, Egor Rumiantsev, Alexander Telepov, Dmitry Protasov, Ilya Shenbin, Anton Alekseev, Mikhail Shirokikh, Sergey Nikolenko, Elena Tutubalina, Artur Kadurin
institutions: St. Petersburg Department of the Steklov Institute of Mathematics

benchmarks.name: WS22
benchmarks.size: ~1.18 million conformations across 10 flexible organic molecules
benchmarks.domain: small organic molecules / conformational and excited-state sampling
benchmarks.description: Generated by combining Wigner sampling around equilibria with geometry interpolation along normal modes, which covers conformational space more broadly than the MD-trajectory sampling behind MD17 — MD frames are temporally correlated and stay near one basin. Provides multiple properties (energies, forces, dipoles, polarizabilities, HOMO/LUMO) for 10 flexible molecules, making it useful for testing sampling-strategy effects on MLIP generalization.
benchmarks.paperTitle: WS22 database, Wigner Sampling and geometry interpolation for configurationally diverse molecular datasets
benchmarks.creators: Max Pinheiro Jr, Shuang Zhang, Pavlo O. Dral, Mario Barbatti

benchmarks.name: GMTKN55
benchmarks.size: 55 benchmark subsets, ~1,505 single-point energies / 2,462 systems
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Mostly CCSD(T)/CBS and higher composite references
benchmarks.description: The gold-standard general benchmark for main-group quantum chemistry methods — 55 curated subsets spanning basic properties, reaction energies, barrier heights, intermolecular and intramolecular non-covalent interactions, aggregated into a single WTMAD-2 score. Originally built to rank density functionals, it is increasingly used to audit MLIPs and foundation models against a target the community already trusts, and is notably harsh on them.
benchmarks.paperTitle: A look at the density functional theory zoo with the advanced GMTKN55 database for general main group thermochemistry, kinetics and noncovalent interactions
benchmarks.creators: Lars Goerigk, Andreas Hansen, Christoph Bauer, Stephan Ehrlich, Asim Najibi, Stefan Grimme

sota.note: Best-performing DFT class in the original assessment; MLIPs generally do substantially worse on the full suite.

benchmarks.name: S66 / S66x8
benchmarks.size: 66 dimers (S66); 528 points across 8 intermolecular distances each (S66x8)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: CCSD(T)/CBS (revised references at higher levels published in 2016 and 2022)
benchmarks.description: The most widely used small non-covalent interaction benchmark, balanced across hydrogen bonding, dispersion and mixed interactions relevant to biomolecular structures. The x8 variant scans 8 intermolecular separations per dimer, giving dissociation curves rather than single minima — which is what exposes whether a model has the right long-range physics or merely the right minimum. Reference values have been revised upward in accuracy twice (Brauer et al. 2016; Santra et al. 2022).
benchmarks.paperTitle: S66: A Well-balanced Database of Benchmark Interaction Energies Relevant to Biomolecular Structures
benchmarks.creators: Jan Řezáč, Kevin E. Riley, Pavel Hobza
institutions: Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry, Czech Academy of Sciences

benchmarks.name: Wiggle150
benchmarks.size: 150 highly strained conformers of 3 molecules (adenosine, benzylpenicillin, efavirenz)
benchmarks.description: A deliberately adversarial 2025 benchmark: conformers distorted far from equilibrium (energies up to ~150 kcal/mol above the minimum) with CCSD(T)/CBS references. Its finding is the point — both common density functionals and neural network potentials degrade sharply on highly strained geometries, despite excellent reported errors on near-equilibrium datasets. Small, cheap, and one of the sharpest available tests of MLIP extrapolation.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Wiggle150: Benchmarking Density Functionals and Neural Network Potentials on Highly Strained Conformers
benchmarks.creators: Rebecca Brew, Joseph Gair, et al. (Sherrill / collaborators)

sota.value: large errors relative to near-equilibrium benchmarks
sota.note: The paper's central result is that NNPs fail on strained conformers; consult the paper for per-model numbers rather than quoting a single figure.

benchmarks.name: QCML
benchmarks.size: 33.5 million DFT calculations and 14.7 billion semi-empirical calculations; ~14 million molecules/conformations, 79 elements
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Multiple DFT levels plus large-scale semi-empirical (GFN2-xTB)
benchmarks.domain: broad chemical space, small molecules and beyond
benchmarks.description: A very large multi-fidelity corpus from Google DeepMind and TU Berlin combining 33.5M DFT reference calculations with 14.7B cheap semi-empirical calculations across 79 elements. Designed explicitly as a pretraining substrate for molecular foundation models, with the semi-empirical tier providing breadth and the DFT tier providing accuracy anchors. Among the broadest element coverages of any molecular dataset.
benchmarks.paperTitle: The QCML dataset, Quantum chemistry reference data from 33.5M DFT and 14.7B semi-empirical calculations
benchmarks.creators: Stefan Ganscha, Oliver T. Unke, Daniel Ahlin, Hartmut Maennel, Sergii Kashubin, Klaus-Robert Müller

sota.note: A 2025 study trained a plain transformer on ~30M QCML structures and reported competitive MD performance, arguing architecture matters less at this data scale.

benchmarks.name: OMol25 (Open Molecules 2025)
benchmarks.size: >100 million DFT calculations; 83 elements; systems up to 350 atoms
benchmarks.domain: broad molecular chemistry: biomolecules, electrolytes, metal complexes, neutral organics
benchmarks.description: The largest and most computationally expensive molecular DFT dataset ever released (billions of CPU-hours), and the current center of gravity for molecular foundation models. Covers 83 elements, explicit charge and spin states, transition-metal complexes, electrolytes and biomolecules up to 350 atoms — deliberately spanning the chemistry that ANI/SPICE-era datasets excluded. Released with evaluation suites and baseline models (UMA, eSEN) via Meta FAIR Chemistry.
benchmarks.paperTitle: The Open Molecules 2025 (OMol25) Dataset, Evaluations, and Models
benchmarks.creators: Daniel S. Levine, Muhammed Shuaibi, Evan Walter Clark Spotte-Smith, Brandon M. Wood, C. Lawrence Zitnick, et al.

sota.model: UMA (Universal Models for Atoms) — uma-s-1p2, uma-m-1p1
sota.note: UMA is a single multi-domain model spanning catalysis, materials, molecules, MOFs; variants at 6.6M/290M active parameters. Verified from the fairchem repo.

sota.value: baseline reported in the OMol25 paper
sota.note: Released as an OMol25 baseline model.

benchmarks.name: MAD (Massive Atomic Diversity)
benchmarks.size: ~95,000 structures (compact by design), spanning 85 elements
benchmarks.domain: universal — organic molecules, inorganic crystals, surfaces, clusters
tasks: foundation model training on a small budget
benchmarks.description: A deliberate counter-argument to the scale race: instead of hundreds of millions of structures, MAD uses ~95k aggressively distorted, deliberately 'unphysical' structures chosen to maximize atomic-environment diversity per sample, all at a single consistent level of theory. Spans molecular and condensed-phase chemistry across 85 elements. Shows that a compact, diversity-optimized dataset can train transferable universal potentials — important given most groups cannot afford OMol25-scale compute.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Massive Atomic Diversity: a compact universal dataset for atomistic machine learning
benchmarks.creators: Arslan Mazitov, Sofiia Chorna, Guillaume Fraux, Marnik Bercx, Giovanni Pizzi, Sandip De, Michele Ceriotti

sota.metric: transferability across molecular and condensed-phase tasks
sota.value: competitive with models trained on far larger datasets
sota.note: Core claim of the paper: dataset diversity substitutes for dataset size.

benchmarks.name: Matbench Discovery
benchmarks.size: WBM test set of ~257k structures screened against ~154k MP training structures; MPtrj / OMat24 / sAlex training corpora
tasks: thermodynamic stability / crystal discovery classification (F1, DAF)
benchmarks.description: A framework evaluating ML models as pre-filters in a high-throughput crystal-discovery campaign, ranking them by their ability to identify thermodynamically stable materials from unrelaxed structures. Now scored primarily by a Combined Performance Score (CPS) weighting F1 (50%), kappa-SRME (40%) and RMSD (10%), which penalizes models that classify well but produce unphysical dynamics. The board has turned over almost completely toward models trained on OMat24+Alexandria+MPtrj ('OAM'); notably eqV2 M, once a top F1 performer (0.917), now sits far down the CPS ranking (0.558) because of its kappa-SRME of 1.77.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Matbench Discovery -- A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions
benchmarks.creators: Janosh Riebesell, Rhys E. A. Goodall, Philipp Benner, Yuan Chiang, Bowen Deng, Gerbrand Ceder, Mark Asta, Alpha A. Lee, Anubhav Jain, Kristin A. Persson

sota.note: Rank 1 by CPS as of 2026-07-17. F1 0.929, kappa-SRME 0.0927, RMSD 0.0575. Added 2026-07-05.
Highest F1 on the board at 0.931; kappa-SRME 0.118, RMSD 0.0595. Added 2026-04-07.
Illustrative of the CPS reweighting: F1 0.917 (competitive with the leaders) but kappa-SRME 1.771 drags CPS to 0.558. Added 2024-10-18.

benchmarks.name: Matbench (v0.1)
benchmarks.size: 14 tasks; 312 (matbench_steels) to 132,752 samples (matbench_mp_e_form)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: mixed — DFT (PBE/GGA, MP-derived) for computed tasks; experimental values for expt_gap, steels, glass
benchmarks.description: The original nested-cross-validation benchmark suite for materials property prediction, released alongside the Automatminer reference algorithm. Deliberately spans composition-only and structure-required tasks and small-to-large data regimes, which made it the standard test of whether GNNs beat classical featurization at low sample counts. Now largely superseded for MLIP work by Matbench Discovery, but still the reference for property regression. 28 algorithms and 180 task submissions on the leaderboard.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Benchmarking Materials Property Prediction Methods: The Matbench Test Set and Automatminer Reference Algorithm
benchmarks.creators: Alexander Dunn, Qi Wang, Alex Ganose, Daniel Dopp, Anubhav Jain

sota.value: leads matbench_steels, matbench_jdft2d, matbench_expt_gap, matbench_dielectric, matbench_glass
sota.note: Dominates the small-data and experimental tasks.

benchmarks.name: Materials Project (MP)
benchmarks.size: ~155k inorganic structures in the MP 2022 snapshot used by Matbench Discovery; database has since grown
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: PBE / PBE+U (VASP), with r2SCAN re-computations for a growing subset
benchmarks.description: The foundational open DFT database for inorganic materials and the source of nearly every downstream MLIP training set in this segment (MPtrj, MPF, MP 2022 snapshots, WBM reference hull). Its GGA/GGA+U mixing corrections define the energy reference that Matbench Discovery and OMat24 adopt.
benchmarks.creators: Kristin A. Persson, Gerbrand Ceder, Anubhav Jain and co-workers

benchmarks.name: MPtrj (Materials Project Trajectory dataset)
benchmarks.size: 1.58M structures from 146k materials (~1.5M inorganic structures per the CHGNet abstract)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: PBE / PBE+U (VASP), MP static + relaxation trajectories
tasks: MLIP pretraining (energies, forces, stresses, magnetic moments)
benchmarks.description: Built by harvesting over ten years of Materials Project static and relaxation trajectories rather than running new DFT — the insight that discarded optimizer intermediates are a free force/stress dataset. Released with CHGNet and uniquely includes magnetic moments, enabling charge-informed potentials. Remains the standard baseline training set on Matbench Discovery and the common denominator against which OMat24/sAlex gains are measured.
benchmarks.paperTitle: CHGNet: Pretrained universal neural network potential for charge-informed atomistic modeling
benchmarks.creators: Bowen Deng, Peichen Zhong, KyuJung Jun, Janosh Riebesell, Kevin Han, Christopher J. Bartel, Gerbrand Ceder

benchmarks.name: MPF.2021.2.8
benchmarks.size: Materials Project snapshot of Feb 2021; ~10^5 structures (exact count unverified)
benchmarks.description: The training set released with M3GNet, and the first widely used 'universal potential' dataset assembled from Materials Project relaxation trajectories. Predates and motivated MPtrj; the naming encodes the Feb 2021 MP snapshot it was cut from.
benchmarks.paperTitle: A Universal Graph Deep Learning Interatomic Potential for the Periodic Table
benchmarks.creators: Chi Chen, Shyue Ping Ong

benchmarks.name: Alexandria
benchmarks.size: millions of DFT-relaxed structures; PBE, PBEsol and SCAN subsets (current exact counts unverified)
benchmarks.description: A very large ML-assisted exploration of the inorganic materials space, notable for offering PBEsol and SCAN subsets alongside PBE — rare among the big databases and useful for functional-transferability studies. Now also distributes MatPES geometries, convex hulls and phonon data. Its subsampled form (sAlex) became a standard co-training set with OMat24.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Large-scale machine-learning-assisted exploration of the whole materials space
benchmarks.creators: Jonathan Schmidt, Noah Hoffmann, Hai-Chen Wang, Pedro Borlido, Pedro J. M. A. Carriço, Tiago F. T. Cerqueira, Silvana Botti, Miguel A. L. Marques

benchmarks.name: sAlex (subsampled Alexandria)
benchmarks.size: 10.4M structures from 3.23M materials
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: PBE / PBE+U, recomputed to be MP/OMat24-compatible
benchmarks.description: A subsampled, MP-compatible cut of Alexandria released with OMat24 so that Alexandria could be mixed with MPtrj and OMat24 under one energy reference. The MPtrj + OMat24 + sAlex ('OAM') combination is the training recipe behind essentially every current Matbench Discovery leader.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) Inorganic Materials Dataset and Models
benchmarks.creators: Luis Barroso-Luque, Muhammed Shuaibi, Xiang Fu, Brandon M. Wood, Misko Dzamba, Meng Gao, Ammar Rizvi, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Zachary W. Ulissi

benchmarks.name: OMat24 (Open Materials 2024)
benchmarks.size: 101M structures from 3.23M materials
benchmarks.description: Meta FAIR's large-scale inorganic materials dataset, built by non-equilibrium sampling (rattled and MD-perturbed structures) rather than relaxation trajectories alone — deliberately covering off-equilibrium regions that MPtrj undersamples. Combined with MPtrj and sAlex it produced the eqV2 models that took the Matbench Discovery lead in 2024, and the OAM recipe still underpins the 2026 leaders.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) Inorganic Materials Dataset and Models
benchmarks.license: MIT (fairchem code); dataset/checkpoint licenses vary by application area
benchmarks.creators: Luis Barroso-Luque, Muhammed Shuaibi, Xiang Fu, Brandon M. Wood, Misko Dzamba, Meng Gao, Ammar Rizvi, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Zachary W. Ulissi

sota.note: kappa-SRME 1.77; strong energetics, weak phonons.

benchmarks.name: OC20 (Open Catalyst 2020)
benchmarks.size: ~1.28M relaxations / ~265M structure-energy frames
benchmarks.description: The dataset that made large-scale MLIP benchmarking mainstream and defined the S2EF/IS2RE/IS2RS task taxonomy still used across catalysis. Its scale (~265M frames) drove the shift from small bespoke potentials to pretrained universal models, and the OC20 evaluation server established held-out leaderboard discipline in the field.
benchmarks.paperTitle: The Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20) Dataset and Community Challenges
benchmarks.creators: Lowik Chanussot, Abhishek Das, Siddharth Goyal, Thibaut Lavril, Muhammed Shuaibi, Morgane Riviere, Kevin Tran, Javier Heras-Domingo, Caleb Ho, Weihua Hu, Aini Palizhati, Anuroop Sriram, Brandon Wood, Junwoong Yoon, Devi Parikh, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Zachary Ulissi

sota.value: leaderboard standings not retrieved — live numbers are behind the OC20 evaluation server
sota.note: Reported here as unverified: the public leaderboard page did not expose current standings on fetch.

benchmarks.name: OC20-Dense
benchmarks.size: dense adsorbate placement evaluation set derived from OC20 (exact size unverified)
tasks: adsorption energy prediction (global minimum over placements)
benchmarks.description: An evaluation set introduced with AdsorbML to test whether MLIPs can find the global-minimum adsorption configuration, not just relax a given one. It reframed the catalysis task from per-structure force accuracy to a search problem, which is what actually matters for screening. Reported here with an unverified paper link.
benchmarks.creators: Janice Lan, Aini Palizhati, Muhammed Shuaibi, Brandon Wood, Zachary Ulissi and co-workers (AdsorbML)

benchmarks.name: OC22 (Open Catalyst 2022)
benchmarks.size: ~62k DFT relaxations / ~9.8M frames (counts unverified)
benchmarks.description: Extends the Open Catalyst effort to oxide electrocatalysts, where PBE+U and open-shell/magnetic behaviour break the assumptions that worked for OC20 metals. Introduced 'total energy' task variants rather than adsorption-referenced energies, making models transferable across compositions.
benchmarks.paperTitle: The Open Catalyst 2022 (OC22) Dataset and Challenges for Oxide Electrocatalysts
benchmarks.creators: Richard Tran, Janice Lan, Muhammed Shuaibi, Brandon M. Wood, Siddharth Goyal, Abhishek Das, Javier Heras-Domingo, Adeesh Kolluru, Ammar Rizvi, Nima Shoghi, Anuroop Sriram, Felix Therrien, Jehad Abed, Oleksandr Voznyy, Edward H. Sargent, Zachary Ulissi, C. Lawrence Zitnick

benchmarks.name: ODAC23 (Open DAC 2023)
benchmarks.size: ~38M DFT calculations on ~8,400 MOFs (counts unverified)
tasks: CO2 and H2O adsorption energy in MOFs
benchmarks.description: The largest MOF-adsorption DFT effort at release, targeting direct air capture sorbent discovery. Distinctive for treating CO2 and H2O co-adsorption — humidity is the practical killer for DAC sorbents — and for the size and flexibility of MOF unit cells, which stress-tests MLIP cutoffs and long-range interactions.
benchmarks.paperTitle: The Open DAC 2023 Dataset and Challenges for Sorbent Discovery in Direct Air Capture
benchmarks.creators: Anuroop Sriram, Sihoon Choi, Xiaohan Yu, Logan M. Brabson, Abhishek Das, Zachary Ulissi, Matt Uyttendaele, Andrew J. Medford, David S. Sholl

benchmarks.name: ODAC25 (Open DAC 2025)
benchmarks.size: not verified
benchmarks.description: The 2025 successor to ODAC23 for direct air capture sorbents.

benchmarks.name: OMC25 (Open Molecular Crystals 2025)
benchmarks.size: not verified
benchmarks.description: Meta FAIR's molecular-crystals dataset, confirmed to exist as the 'OMC' application area supported by fairchem and the UMA models. Molecular crystal polymorph ranking needs sub-kJ/mol accuracy and correct dispersion, making it one of the hardest MLIP targets.

benchmarks.name: MatPES
benchmarks.size: ~400,000 structures sampled from 281M MD snapshots spanning 16 billion atomic environments
benchmarks.description: Argues against the scale-maximalist trend: rather than dumping every trajectory frame, MatPES carefully subsamples ~400k structures from 281M MD snapshots to cover the PES efficiently, and provides r2SCAN alongside PBE — a meaningfully better functional than the GGA that MPtrj/OMat24 rely on. Positions data quality and functional accuracy, not raw frame count, as the binding constraint on foundation potentials.
benchmarks.paperTitle: A Foundational Potential Energy Surface Dataset for Materials
benchmarks.creators: Aaron D. Kaplan, Runze Liu, Ji Qi, Tsz Wai Ko, Bowen Deng, Janosh Riebesell, Gerbrand Ceder, Kristin A. Persson, Shyue Ping Ong

benchmarks.name: WBM dataset
benchmarks.size: ~257k relaxed structures generated by elemental substitution (exact count unverified)
tasks: out-of-distribution stability prediction (test set for Matbench Discovery)
benchmarks.description: Generated by iterative elemental substitution on Materials Project prototypes over five rounds, giving a genuinely out-of-distribution test set whose later rounds drift progressively further from MP. That drift is precisely why Matbench Discovery adopted it as the held-out set: it measures extrapolation to novel chemistries rather than interpolation within MP. Named for authors Wang, Botti and Marques.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Predicting stable crystalline compounds using chemical similarity
benchmarks.creators: Hai-Chen Wang, Silvana Botti, Miguel A. L. Marques

benchmarks.name: OQMD (Open Quantum Materials Database)
benchmarks.size: 1,407,395 entries (as of July 2026)
benchmarks.description: One of the three original large open DFT databases (with MP and AFLOW), built around ICSD prototypes plus systematic decoration of common structure types. Its formation-energy and hull data remain a standard cross-check against MP, and it is a major constituent of aggregated sets like LeMat-Bulk. Entry count and CC-BY-4.0 license verified live.
benchmarks.creators: Chris Wolverton and co-workers

benchmarks.name: AFLOW
benchmarks.size: not verified (site did not expose counts on fetch)
benchmarks.description: A high-throughput DFT framework and database built on an explicit prototype library and a standardized calculation protocol, notable for the AFLOW-AEL/AGL modules producing elastic and quasi-harmonic thermal properties at scale. Its 'agm-' identifiers appear as a source in aggregated datasets such as LeMat-Bulk.
benchmarks.creators: Stefano Curtarolo and co-workers

benchmarks.name: NOMAD
benchmarks.size: 19,424,588 uploaded entries / 4,346,100 represented materials / 129.1 TB (as of July 2026)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: heterogeneous — aggregates output from 60+ codes and many functionals
benchmarks.domain: inorganic crystals and general computational materials science
benchmarks.description: Less a benchmark than the field's archive layer: a repository that ingests raw output from over 60 simulation codes and normalizes it into a common schema, making otherwise-unpublishable intermediate calculations reusable. Its heterogeneity of functionals and codes is both its value (breadth) and its limitation (no single consistent level of theory for MLIP training). Counts and license verified live.
benchmarks.creators: Matthias Scheffler, Claudia Draxl and the NOMAD Laboratory
institutions: Fritz Haber Institute of the Max Planck Society

benchmarks.name: JARVIS-DFT
benchmarks.size: not verified (database page required login on fetch)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: OptB88vdW (van der Waals); TBmBJ for improved band gaps; some SCAN
tasks: band gaps, elastic, dielectric, topological and solar properties
benchmarks.description: NIST's DFT database, distinguished from MP/OQMD/AFLOW by its choice of the OptB88vdW functional — which handles layered and 2D materials properly — and by TBmBJ band gaps that are far closer to experiment than GGA. That makes it the reference of choice for 2D materials and for band-gap tasks (its jdft2d exfoliation set feeds Matbench).
benchmarks.creators: Kamal Choudhary, Francesca Tavazza and co-workers
institutions: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

benchmarks.name: JARVIS-Leaderboard
benchmarks.size: large multi-category benchmark spanning AI, electronic-structure, force-field, quantum and experimental categories
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: multiple — includes DFT (OptB88vdW, TBmBJ), QMC and experimental references
benchmarks.domain: inorganic crystals, 2D materials, broad materials design
benchmarks.description: Unusually broad in scope: rather than ranking ML models on one task, it benchmarks entire methods — DFT functionals, force fields, QMC, and even experiments — against common references, with contributions reproducible via a standardized submission format. Useful as a sanity check on how much of an MLIP's error is inherited from its underlying DFT reference. 38 authors, led by Kamal Choudhary.
benchmarks.paperTitle: JARVIS-Leaderboard: A Large Scale Benchmark of Materials Design Methods
benchmarks.creators: Kamal Choudhary, Daniel Wines, Kangming Li, Kevin F. Garrity, Francesca Tavazza and 33 co-authors
institutions: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

benchmarks.name: HME21 (High-temperature Multi-Element 2021)
benchmarks.size: ~25k structures spanning 45 elements (count unverified)
tasks: MLIP pretraining and evaluation across arbitrary element combinations
benchmarks.description: The dataset behind PFP (PreFerred Potential), the model powering Matlantis — and one of the earliest serious attempts at a genuinely universal potential covering arbitrary combinations of 45 elements. Notable as an industrial, commercially deployed counterpart to the academic universal-potential line, generated by high-temperature MD sampling to cover disordered multi-element environments.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Towards Universal Neural Network Potential for Material Discovery Applicable to Arbitrary Combination of 45 Elements
benchmarks.creators: So Takamoto, Chikashi Shinagawa, Daisuke Motoki, Kosuke Nakago and co-workers

sota.note: Commercially deployed via the Matlantis platform.

benchmarks.name: OpenLAM
benchmarks.size: 163M structures (as reported as a training set on Matbench Discovery)
benchmarks.description: The open large-atomic-model initiative associated with the DeepModeling/AISI ecosystem (DPA-family potentials), contributing one of the largest structure counts of any training set appearing on Matbench Discovery at 163M structures. Size verified from the Matbench Discovery models page; paper, license and exact level of theory unverified.
benchmarks.creators: DeepModeling / AI for Science Institute community

benchmarks.name: MatterGen (and its benchmarks)
benchmarks.size: trained on Alexandria + MP-derived data; benchmark suite for generative models
benchmarks.description: A diffusion-based generative model for inorganic crystals that also established the evaluation conventions now standard for generative materials work — notably the stable/unique/novel (SUN) rate and DFT-verified stability rather than proxy metrics. Included here because its benchmark protocol, not just the model, is what the field adopted. Verified as v1 Dec 2023.
benchmarks.paperTitle: MatterGen: a generative model for inorganic materials design
benchmarks.creators: Claudio Zeni, Robert Pinsler, Daniel Zügner, Andrew Fowler, Matthew Horton, Xiang Fu, Sasha Shysheya, Jonathan Crabbé, Lixin Sun, Jake Smith, Bichlien Nguyen, Hannes Schulz, Sarah Lewis, Chin-Wei Huang, Ziheng Lu, Yichi Zhou, Han Yang, Hongxia Hao, Jielan Li, Ryota Tomioka, Tian Xie

benchmarks.name: LeMaterial / LeMat-Bulk
benchmarks.size: ~6.7M rows across four subsets; largest subset 'compatible_pbe' at 5.34M entries
benchmarks.description: An open effort to reconcile Materials Project, AFLOW and OQMD into one deduplicated, energy-compatible dataset — addressing the practical problem that the big three databases use incompatible settings and corrections, so naively concatenating them corrupts hull distances. Provides 'compatible_pbe' subsets with a consistent reference. Size, license and PBE level verified live on HuggingFace.
benchmarks.creators: LeMaterial (Hugging Face / Entalpic collaboration)

benchmarks.name: TorchSim (torch-sim)
benchmarks.size: Simulation engine; supports MACE, FairChem, SevenNet, ORB, MatterSim, GraphPES and other MLIP backends
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Model-agnostic (whatever the loaded MLIP was trained at)
tasks: Batched molecular dynamics (NVE, NVT Langevin, NPT Langevin) across thousands of structures simultaneously
Batched structure relaxation (FIRE, gradient descent, unit-cell filters)
benchmarks.description: TorchSim's insight is that the bottleneck for MLIP-driven high-throughput simulation was never the model — it was the simulation loop, which in ASE runs one structure at a time in Python while the GPU sits idle. By rewriting MD/relaxation primitives in PyTorch with automatic GPU batching, it reports up to 100x speedup over ASE with the same potentials. This is the piece of infrastructure that makes MLIP-based screening of thousands of structures routine rather than a multi-week job. Published in AI for Science (2025).
benchmarks.paperTitle: TorchSim: An efficient atomistic simulation engine in PyTorch
benchmarks.creators: Orion Cohen, Janosh Riebesell, Rhys Goodall, Muhammed Shuaibi (Kolluru), Stefano Falletta, Curtis Krause, Abhijeet Gangan, Colindres, Gerbrand Ceder

sota.metric: speedup vs. ASE with popular MLIPs
sota.note: Speedup is from GPU batching; the gain is largest for many small systems and shrinks for a single large system.

benchmarks.name: mlipx (Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential eXploration)
benchmarks.size: Recipe library; supports arbitrary ASE-compatible MLIP calculators
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Model-agnostic; comparisons are relative to user-supplied DFT or experimental references
tasks: Side-by-side model comparison with interactive ZnDraw visualization
benchmarks.description: mlipx is BASF's industrial answer to the question 'which MLIP should I actually use for my problem?' — deliberately scoped not as a global leaderboard but as a reproducible recipe library you point at your own systems. Its design bet is that MLIP selection is inherently application-specific, so the useful artifact is a standardized, version-controlled comparison workflow rather than a ranking. It is lightweight by construction (bundles no MLIP dependencies; you install the calculators you want) and integrates with ZnDraw for interactive inspection. Published in J. Phys.: Condens. Matter.
benchmarks.paperTitle: mlipx: Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential eXploration
benchmarks.creators: Sheena Agarwal, Sandip De, Fabian Zills, and colleagues at BASF

sota.model: n/a — evaluation harness, not a ranked benchmark
sota.note: mlipx intentionally does not publish a single global ranking; it produces per-application comparisons.

benchmarks.name: MLIP Arena
benchmarks.size: Benchmark platform with modular task suites; evaluates dozens of published MLIP foundation models
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Deliberately not DFT-reference-only — evaluates against physical laws, experimental observables, and thermodynamic properties
tasks: MD — molecular dynamics stability (incl. under extreme conditions)
NEB — nudged elastic band / reaction barriers
Physics-awareness checks: energy conservation, force smoothness, homonuclear diatomic curves, chemical reactivity
benchmarks.description: MLIP Arena is the field's most pointed critique of its own evaluation culture: it argues that ranking MLIPs by DFT force MAE on held-out test sets is close to meaningless, because low MAE routinely coexists with unphysical behavior — non-conservative forces, exploding MD, nonsensical diatomic dissociation curves. Instead it evaluates physical soundness and practical utility directly, architecture- and training-data-agnostic, on a Hugging Face Space with a live leaderboard. Its diatomic-curve diagnostics in particular have embarrassed several widely-deployed foundation potentials. NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight (top 3.5%). This is essential reading for anyone about to report an MAE number as evidence of quality.
benchmarks.paperTitle: MLIP Arena: Advancing Fairness and Transparency in Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials via an Open, Accessible Benchmark Platform
benchmarks.creators: Yuan Chiang, Tobias Kreiman, Christine Zhang, Matthew C. Kuner, Elizabeth Weaver, Ishan Amin, Hyunsoo Park, Yunsung Lim, Jihan Kim, Daryl Chrzan, Aron Walsh, Samuel M. Blau, Mark Asta, Aditi S. Krishnapriyan

sota.note: The platform's core finding is that no single model wins across tasks, and that DFT-error rankings do not predict physical-soundness rankings. Consult the Hugging Face Space for current standings rather than quoting a fixed winner.

benchmarks.name: kappa-SRME / PhononDB thermal-conductivity benchmark
benchmarks.size: phonon benchmark set derived from PhononDB (exact count unverified)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: PBE (VASP), harmonic and anharmonic force constants
benchmarks.domain: inorganic crystals — phonons and thermal transport
tasks: lattice thermal conductivity prediction via Wigner/Boltzmann transport
benchmarks.description: The symmetric relative mean error on lattice thermal conductivity, now a headline axis of Matbench Discovery. Its importance is diagnostic: it requires accurate second- and third-order force constants, so it detects models that fit energies well but have a subtly wrong PES curvature — eqV2 M scores F1 0.917 yet kappa-SRME 1.77, while 2026 leaders reach ~0.09. Lower is better; 2.0 is the worst possible score. Built on Togo's PhononDB reference set. Paper link unverified.
benchmarks.creators: Balázs Póta, Paramvir Ahlawat, Gábor Csányi, Michele Simoncelli (kappa-SRME); Atsushi Togo (PhononDB)

benchmarks.description: The foundational benchmark suite for molecular machine learning, curating 17 public datasets under a single API with prescribed metrics and splits (random, scaffold, stratified, time). Its central methodological contribution was popularizing the scaffold split as a proxy for out-of-distribution generalization, which remains the default protocol for property-prediction papers. It ships as part of DeepChem with reference implementations of ECFP, graph convolutions, weave, and Deep Tensor Neural Networks. Despite documented issues — small sample sizes, label noise in ClinTox/SIDER, and high split-seed variance — it is still the most-reported benchmark in the molecular representation-learning literature.

Its key design decision is the Benchmark Group abstraction: fixed splits (crucially scaffold and time-based, which surface distributional shift), fixed metrics, and 5-seed mean±std reporting, which makes ADMET results genuinely comparable across papers in a way MoleculeNet never achieved. The ADMET Benchmark Group in particular has become the de facto standard for ADMET model papers. Important caveat: the leaderboards are self-reported, so entries are not independently reproduced.

benchmarks.description: The largest and most influential quantum-property regression benchmark in graph ML, run as a KDD Cup 2021 track that drew 500+ team registrations. Its defining feature is the train-time-3D / inference-time-2D asymmetry in v2, which made it the proving ground for 3D-denoising pretraining, noisy-node regularization, and geometry-prediction auxiliary losses — techniques that then propagated back into MLIP and molecular foundation-model work. v1 was deprecated in favor of v2 after leakage and duplicate issues were found. Because the label is a single DFT scalar at a modest level of theory, low MAE here should not be read as chemical accuracy in any physical sense.

benchmarks.description: Polaris is a cross-industry response to the credibility crisis in molecular ML benchmarking — the recognition that MoleculeNet-style leaderboards had been optimized past the point of meaning. Its central claim is method-comparison rigor: industry-certified datasets, blinded test sets held by the platform rather than published, and explicit guidelines against the split/metric shopping that inflates published numbers. The consortium (Recursion, AstraZeneca, Relay, Pfizer, Merck, Nimbus, Blueprint, J&J, Novartis, Bayer, Valence Labs) is the point: it unlocks proprietary-quality assay data that academic benchmarks structurally cannot obtain. Its ASAP Discovery antiviral challenges are prospective rather than retrospective, which is rare and valuable.

benchmarks.name: PLINDER (Protein-Ligand INteraction Dataset and Evaluation Resource)

tasks: Protein-ligand docking and co-folding evaluation with leakage-controlled splits
Similarity-aware train/val/test splitting (protein sequence, pocket, ligand, and interaction-fingerprint similarity simultaneously)

benchmarks.description: PLINDER exists because the field's protein-ligand benchmarks were quietly broken: PDBBind-style time splits leave severe train/test leakage, and reported docking successes were substantially memorization. Its contribution is not just scale but the similarity-aware splitting machinery — it measures leakage along protein, pocket, ligand, and interaction axes at once and constructs splits that actually hold out novelty. It is co-organized by the CASP organizers, and is the intended data substrate for the next generation of co-folding models. Any 2025+ docking claim that does not report on PLINDER-style splits should be read skeptically.

benchmarks.name: PoseBusters
benchmarks.size: PoseBusters Benchmark set: 428 protein-ligand crystal structures released after 2021 (post-PDBBind-cutoff), curated for quality; plus the PoseBusters validity-check suite itself
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: N/A — experimental crystal structures; validity checks use RDKit/UFF geometry criteria
tasks: Docking pose validity checking: chemical (bond lengths/angles, aromatic ring flatness, stereochemistry, internal energy) and physical (protein-ligand steric clash, volume overlap, ligand inside the pocket)
Docking accuracy evaluation: RMSD < 2 A AND passes all PoseBusters checks ('PB-valid') — the stricter joint metric
Generalization test: performance on structures with sequences novel relative to the training cutoff
benchmarks.description: PoseBusters is the paper that punctured the deep-learning docking bubble. Its argument is simple and devastating: RMSD < 2 A alone is a broken metric, because DL methods routinely achieve it while producing poses with impossible bond geometry, non-flat aromatic rings, and steric clashes through the protein. Once you require physical validity AND accuracy, no deep-learning method of that era beat classical docking (they benchmarked DeepDock, DiffDock, EquiBind, TankBind, Uni-Mol against Vina/Gold). The 'PB-valid' metric and the 428-structure benchmark set have since become mandatory reporting for any docking or co-folding paper, and PoseBusters-style validity filtering is now built into AlphaFold3-era evaluation.
benchmarks.paperTitle: PoseBusters: AI-based docking methods fail to generate physically valid poses or generalise to novel sequences
benchmarks.license: MIT (code); benchmark data on Zenodo record 8278563

benchmarks.description: PDBbind is the long-running curated collection pairing PDB crystal structures with experimentally measured binding affinities, and CASF-2016 is its associated four-axis benchmark (scoring / ranking / docking / screening power) built on a 285-complex core set clustered into 57 targets with 5 ligands each. Together they were the standard for structure-based affinity prediction for over a decade. The critical caveat for a PhD student: the widely used PDBbind v2016/v2020 splits are severely leaky, and multiple audits have shown that models scoring well can do so by memorizing protein identity rather than learning interactions — a ligand-only or protein-only baseline recovers much of the reported performance. Treat PDBbind numbers as historical context and use PLINDER-style splits for new claims.

benchmarks.name: OpenProteinSet
benchmarks.size: > 16 million multiple sequence alignments (MSAs); ~140k PDB-associated MSAs + ~16M UniClust30 cluster MSAs, with structural homologs and AlphaFold2 predictions

benchmarks.description: OpenProteinSet removed the single largest barrier to open protein-structure-prediction research: the compute cost of generating MSAs, which dominates AlphaFold2 training and had kept retraining out of reach for academic groups. It provides 16M+ precomputed MSAs plus structural homologs and AF2 predictions, and is the data substrate behind OpenFold — the trainable PyTorch AF2 reproduction whose retraining experiments produced the notable insight that AF2 learns structure in a spatially-coarse-to-fine order and generalizes from surprisingly little data. For MLIP researchers it matters as the template for what open, at-scale biomolecular training data looks like.

benchmarks.size: 19,443 curated ligands with QM properties; 16,972 protein-ligand complexes with MD simulations (~133 GiB MD data, ~8 ns per system, ~0.3 GiB QM, 6 GiB electronic densities, 55 GiB restart/topology files)

benchmarks.domain: biomolecules / protein-ligand complexes, structure-based drug discovery
tasks: Binding affinity prediction from dynamic (MD) rather than static structural information
QM property prediction on curated ligands (partial charges, electronic densities)
Structural refinement — correcting protonation states, geometry errors, and ligand chemistry in PDB-derived complexes
benchmarks.description: MISATO's premise is that static crystal structures throw away the information that actually determines binding, and that PDB-derived protein-ligand complexes are riddled with chemistry errors nobody corrects. It addresses both: QM calculations to fix and characterize 19,443 ligands, and MD simulations of 16,972 complexes to supply the dynamics. It ships AI-ready HDF5 with PyTorch dataloaders and baseline models, lowering the barrier for ML researchers who don't run MD. Together with mdCATH and ATLAS it forms the 2024-era shift from structure datasets to ensemble/dynamics datasets — the data regime that biomolecular MLIPs actually need.

benchmarks.description: ATLAS is a standardized, non-redundant MD database covering 1,938 protein structures selected to span ECOD structural diversity, each simulated in triplicate for 100 ns with a consistent protocol. The consistency is the point: unlike opportunistic collections of published trajectories, ATLAS lets you compare across proteins without confounding force-field and protocol differences. It has become the standard evaluation set for the wave of generative conformational-ensemble models (AlphaFlow, ConfDiff, Str2Str and successors), which report ensemble observables against ATLAS reference trajectories. Note the CC-BY-NC license — it restricts commercial use, unlike mdCATH.

benchmarks.name: mdCATH
benchmarks.size: 5,398 protein domains, 5 replicates x 5 temperatures (320-450 K) each = ~134,950 trajectories, > 62 milliseconds of aggregate simulation time
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Classical all-atom MD, CHARMM22* force field, implicit solvent, ACEMD/GPU
benchmarks.domain: biomolecules / proteins, molecular dynamics and thermodynamics
tasks: Training ML surrogates for MD (transition density / timestep-jumping models)
benchmarks.description: mdCATH is the largest open protein MD dataset by aggregate simulation time (62+ ms), covering 5,398 CATH domains at five temperatures from 320 K to 450 K. The temperature ladder is its distinguishing feature — it captures unfolding pathways and thermodynamics, not just near-native fluctuation, which is what makes it usable for learning transferable dynamics rather than a single basin. It has rapidly become the training substrate for the MD-surrogate generative model line (DeepJump, ATMOS, DynaMode and others), which aim for ~1000x acceleration over explicit MD. The tradeoff to be aware of: implicit solvent and CHARMM22* mean the reference dynamics are cheap but not gold-standard.

benchmarks.license: Open (see HuggingFace dataset card); published in Scientific Data (2024)

benchmarks.size: Adaptive-sampling MD ensembles of intrinsically disordered protein-partner systems; the canonical c-Myb/KIX system comprises hundreds of microseconds of aggregate adaptive sampling
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Classical all-atom MD with adaptive/online-learning sampling (ACEMD; CHARMM/AMBER-family force fields), explicit solvent
benchmarks.domain: biomolecules / intrinsically disordered proteins, coupled folding and binding
tasks: Markov state model / kinetics estimation for coupled folding-binding
Distinguishing conformational selection vs. induced fit mechanisms
Benchmarking coarse-grained and ML force fields on disordered systems (where most MLIPs and structure predictors fail)
benchmarks.description: This is a smaller and less formalized 'benchmark' than the others, but it occupies an important niche: intrinsically disordered proteins that fold only upon binding are the systems where AlphaFold-style single-structure prediction is definitionally inapplicable and where ML force fields are least validated. The De Fabritiis-lab work on c-Myb transactivation domain binding to the KIX domain of CBP is the reference study, reconstructing the full binding-and-folding landscape with online-learning adaptive sampling and finding a mixture of conformational selection (N-terminal) and induced fit (C-terminal). For a PhD student, treat this as an evaluation target rather than a packaged leaderboard: it is the hard case that exposes whether a biomolecular MLIP has learned physics or memorized folds.

benchmarks.description: ASE is the substrate the entire MLIP ecosystem is built on, and its historical importance is the Calculator abstraction: by defining a single interface for 'given an Atoms object, return energy and forces', it made MLIPs drop-in replacements for DFT codes. Every foundation potential ships an ASE calculator; every benchmark harness (mlipx, MLIP Arena, torch-sim) consumes them. Its weakness is exactly what torch-sim was built to fix — the Python-level, one-structure-at-a-time loop is a severe bottleneck for GPU-backed models. The canonical reference is Larsen et al., J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 29, 273002 (2017).

benchmarks.name: i-PI
benchmarks.size: Universal force engine; v3.x as of 2024-2026
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Model-agnostic client-server design — any code (DFT or MLIP) can serve forces
tasks: Path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) — nuclear quantum effects
Ring polymer MD / centroid MD, thermostatted RPMD
Path integral coarse-graining and PIGLET accelerated quantum thermostats
Geometry optimization, phonons, instanton rate theory
Universal socket interface to force providers (CP2K, FHI-aims, LAMMPS, and MLIP codes)
benchmarks.description: i-PI is where nuclear quantum effects meet MLIPs. Its client-server architecture is the key design choice: i-PI handles the (cheap) nuclear propagation in Python while any external code computes forces over a socket, which means an MLIP written in PyTorch gets full PIMD, RPMD, and quantum-thermostat machinery for free. Since NQEs matter enormously for hydrogen-containing systems — water, proton transfer, biomolecules — i-PI is the standard route for MLIP practitioners who need more than classical dynamics. Version 3 (Litman et al., J. Chem. Phys. 161, 062504, 2024) substantially broadened its scope beyond PIMD.
benchmarks.paperTitle: i-PI 3.0: A flexible and efficient framework for advanced atomistic simulations
benchmarks.license: MIT / GPL (multiple licenses per component — see the licenses folder in the repo)
benchmarks.creators: Yair Litman, Venkat Kapil, Yotam M. Y. Feldman, Davide Tisi, Tomislav Begusic, Karen Fidanyan, Guillaume Fraux, Jacob Higer, Matthias Kellner, Tao E. Li, Eszter S. Pos, Elia Stocco, George Trenins, Barak Hirshberg, Mariana Rossi, Michele Ceriotti, and colleagues

benchmarks.name: OpenMM (+ openmm-torch / openmm-ml)
benchmarks.size: v8.x (8.5.2 as of June 2026)
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Classical MM force fields (AMBER, CHARMM, OpenFF) with ML/MM hybrid support via openmm-torch
tasks: Custom forces and integrators (its distinguishing capability)
ML/MM hybrid simulation: ML potential on the ligand or QM region, MM elsewhere, via openmm-torch
Drop-in ML potentials (ANI-2x, MACE-OFF, Nutmeg, AIMNet2) via openmm-ml
benchmarks.description: OpenMM is the MD engine through which most biomolecular MLIP work actually reaches a simulation. Its architectural advantage — custom forces and integrators defined at the Python level, JIT-compiled to GPU kernels — is precisely what made the openmm-torch bridge possible, letting a PyTorch MLIP act as a force term inside a conventional biomolecular simulation. The openmm-ml layer then makes ML/MM hybrid setups (ML on the ligand, MM on the protein and solvent) a few lines of code, which is the dominant practical pattern for drug-discovery MLIP applications today. The same Stanford/Chodera-adjacent community produced SPICE and Nutmeg, and the tooling is designed to interlock.
benchmarks.paperTitle: OpenMM 8: Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Machine Learning Potentials
