benchmarks.name: TorchMD-NET
benchmarks.size: Framework; ships TensorNet, TensorNet2, and (deprecated) Equivariant Transformer / Transformer / GNN architectures
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Model-agnostic training framework; pretrained models target ANI-1x, SPICE, QM9, MD17 levels of theory
tasks: Training NNPs on energies and forces (QM9, MD17, ANI-1x, SPICE, custom HDF5)
Deployment as TorchScript modules into ACEMD, OpenMM, and TorchMD
benchmarks.description: TorchMD-NET is the De Fabritiis lab's NNP training-and-deployment stack, and its significance for biomolecular work is the deployment half: models are exposed as plain PyTorch/TorchScript modules that drop directly into GPU MD engines, closing the usual gap between 'trained a potential' and 'ran a simulation'. Architecturally it introduced the Equivariant Transformer (Tholke & De Fabritiis, ICLR 2022) and later TensorNet (Simeon & De Fabritiis, NeurIPS 2023), which achieves O(3)-equivariance via Cartesian rank-2 tensors rather than spherical harmonics — notably more parameter- and data-efficient. The 2.0 release (Pelaez et al., J. Chem. Phys. 2024) focused on making inference fast enough for production MD.
benchmarks.paperTitle: TorchMD-Net 2.0: Fast Neural Network Potentials for Molecular Simulations
benchmarks.creators: Raul P. Pelaez, Guillem Simeon, Raimondas Galvelis, Antonio Mirarchi, Peter Eastman, Stefan Doerr, Philipp Tholke, Thomas E. Markland, Gianni De Fabritiis

sota.metric: MD17 / rMD17 force MAE; QM9 property MAE
sota.value: SOTA at publication with notably fewer parameters
sota.note: Simeon & De Fabritiis, NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2306.06482. Cartesian rank-2 tensor equivariance rather than spherical harmonics.
Tholke & De Fabritiis, ICLR 2022, arXiv 2202.02541. Now marked deprecated in the repo in favor of TensorNet.

benchmarks.name: JAX MD
benchmarks.size: Differentiable MD library
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Model-agnostic; ships classical potentials (LJ, EAM, Morse) and neural network potentials (BehlerParrinello, GNNs)
tasks: MD simulators: NVE, NVT (Nose-Hoover, Langevin), NPT, FIRE minimization, Brownian
Spatial partitioning / neighbor lists that are themselves differentiable
Meta-optimization: differentiating through entire trajectories to fit potentials to observables
Automatic vectorization and hardware acceleration (CPU/GPU/TPU via XLA)
benchmarks.description: JAX MD's contribution is conceptual as much as practical: by writing MD in JAX, the whole trajectory becomes differentiable, so you can take gradients of a simulation observable with respect to potential parameters. That enables top-down force-field fitting — train a potential to reproduce experimental structure factors or elastic constants rather than DFT forces — which is otherwise very hard. It also made TPU-scale MD accessible and heavily influenced downstream JAX-based MLIP codes (JAX-MD-based NequIP ports, MACE-JAX, Allegro-JAX). Its practical adoption has been narrower than the PyTorch ecosystem, but its ideas propagated widely.
benchmarks.paperTitle: JAX M.D. A Framework for Differentiable Physics
benchmarks.creators: Samuel S. Schoenholz, Ekin D. Cubuk

sota.note: NeurIPS 2020. arXiv id 1912.04232 is the preprint of this work — I did not independently fetch that arXiv page in this pass, so verify the id if you cite the preprint rather than the NeurIPS version.

benchmarks.name: MACE (mace-torch)
benchmarks.size: Framework + foundation model family: MACE-MP (materials), MACE-OFF (organic/biomolecular, SPICE-trained), MACE-OMOL, MACE-Polar
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Model-dependent: MACE-MP trained on Materials Project PBE(+U); MACE-OFF trained on SPICE at wB97M-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVPPD
benchmarks.domain: software/harness (MLIP training framework and foundation models)
tasks: Training equivariant MLIPs with higher-order (body-ordered) equivariant message passing
Foundation-model inference across the periodic table (MACE-MP-0/0b/1) and organic chemistry (MACE-OFF23/24)
Finetuning foundation potentials on domain-specific data
ASE calculator, LAMMPS, and OpenMM deployment
benchmarks.description: MACE is included here as a harness because mace-torch has become de facto infrastructure rather than merely a published architecture: it is the reference implementation that MLIP Arena, mlipx, and torch-sim all benchmark against, and MACE-OFF is the biomolecular foundation potential most commonly dropped into OpenMM for ML/MM drug-discovery workflows. Its architectural contribution is combining the ACE body-ordered expansion with equivariant message passing, reaching high body order in only two message-passing layers — which is why it is both accurate and fast enough to deploy. Note the licensing split: MIT code, but several pretrained checkpoints carry the more restrictive ASL license.
benchmarks.paperTitle: MACE: Higher Order Equivariant Message Passing Neural Networks for Fast and Accurate Force Fields
benchmarks.license: MIT (code); pretrained models vary — some ASL (Academic Software License), some MIT
benchmarks.creators: Ilyes Batatia, David P. Kovacs, Gregor N. C. Simm, Christoph Ortner, Gabor Csanyi

sota.metric: SPICE test set energy/force MAE; biomolecular MD stability
sota.note: The most-used organic/biomolecular foundation potential; deployable in OpenMM via openmm-ml. arXiv id for MACE-OFF is separate from the base MACE paper — verify before citing.
Materials-domain foundation model; out of scope for this biomolecular segment but the same codebase.

benchmarks.name: FAIRChem (fairchem)
benchmarks.size: Centralized repo for FAIR Chemistry datasets/models: OC20 (~1.2M relaxations / 265M structures), OC22, OC25, OMat24, OMol25, ODAC, OMC, UMA models
benchmarks.levelOfTheory: Dataset-dependent: OC20/OC22 RPBE and PBE+U; OMat24 PBE/PBE+U (VASP); OMol25 wB97M-V/def2-TZVPD (molecules, ORCA)
benchmarks.domain: software/harness (models, datasets, and inference for chemistry/materials); OMol25 subset is molecules/biomolecules
tasks: MLIP training and inference across catalysis (OC20/OC22/OC25), inorganic materials (OMat24), molecules and polymers (OMol25), MOFs/DAC (ODAC), molecular crystals (OMC)
UMA (Universal Model for Atoms) — single model spanning all domains via mixture-of-linear-experts
S2EF (structure to energy and forces), IS2RE, IS2RS tasks
ASE calculator interface for all pretrained checkpoints
benchmarks.description: FAIRChem is Meta FAIR's consolidated chemistry stack, and its relevance to this biomolecular segment is chiefly OMol25 — a very large molecular dataset computed at wB97M-V/def2-TZVPD covering biomolecules, electrolytes, and metal complexes including charged and open-shell species, which is the most direct competitor to SPICE as a biomolecular MLIP training set. The UMA models are the more provocative contribution: a single potential claiming competence across catalysis, materials, molecules, and MOFs simultaneously, which tests whether 'foundation model' means anything in this field. Be aware of the v1-to-v2 breaking change: v2 is incompatible with older pretrained checkpoints, and model/checkpoint licenses differ from the MIT code license.

benchmarks.name: NeurIPS (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
benchmarks.description: The flagship annual ML conference and the single most important venue for MLIP methods papers — NequIP, Allegro, GemNet, DimeNet++, MACE and the Open Catalyst challenges all appeared here or in its workshops. NeurIPS 2026 is the 40th edition, held in Sydney, Australia, December 6-12, 2026, with satellite sites in Atlanta and Paris, December 9-13. The workshop track (AI4Mat, ML4PS, AI4Science) is where most atomistic ML community activity concentrates. Verified from the official site.

benchmarks.name: ICML (International Conference on Machine Learning)
benchmarks.description: Second of the big-three ML conferences and a major home for equivariant-network and molecular-representation theory papers. ICML 2026 is the 43rd edition, held July 6-11, 2026 at COEX in Seoul, South Korea: July 6 for expo/tutorials, July 7-9 main conference, July 10-11 workshops. Relevant workshops include ML4LMS (Machine Learning for Life and Material Sciences) and the Computational Biology workshop. Verified from the official site.

benchmarks.name: ICLR (International Conference on Learning Representations)
benchmarks.description: Open-review conference focused on representation learning; historically the venue for DimeNet, SphereNet, and much geometric deep learning for molecules. ICLR 2026 is the 14th edition, April 23-27, 2026, at the Riocentro Convention Center in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Hosts the MLDD (Machine Learning for Drug Discovery) and AI4Mat workshops. Verified from the official site.

benchmarks.name: AI4Mat — AI for Accelerated Materials Design Workshop
benchmarks.description: The central workshop bringing AI researchers and materials scientists together, covering crystalline and amorphous solids, glasses, molecules, nanomaterials and devices. Inaugurated at NeurIPS 2022 and run at NeurIPS 2023, AI4Mat-BOKU-2024 (Vienna), NeurIPS 2024 (Vancouver), ICLR 2025 (Singapore, its first in Asia), NeurIPS 2025, and ICLR 2026 (Rio, April 26, 2026). The 2026 edition themes are reinforcement learning / feedback-driven approaches and cross-modal unified materials representations. Verified from the workshop site.

benchmarks.name: ML4PS — Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences Workshop (NeurIPS)
benchmarks.description: Long-running NeurIPS workshop covering ML across physics, chemistry, astronomy and materials, and a frequent first home for MLIP and simulation-surrogate work. It has run annually alongside NeurIPS for most of the past decade and is one of the largest NeurIPS workshops by submission count.

benchmarks.name: MoML — Molecular Machine Learning Conference
benchmarks.description: A biannual gathering of academic and industry researchers on ML for molecular modeling, molecular interactions, and therapeutic design, organized by the MIT Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health. Held in honor of Octavian-Eugen Ganea (1987-2022). Editions documented in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 (at both MIT and Mila); the 2026 edition, scheduled for October 14, 2026, is the 8th iteration. Verified from the official site.

benchmarks.name: LoG — Learning on Graphs Conference
benchmarks.description: Annual conference on machine learning on graphs and geometry with an explicit emphasis on high-quality peer review — highly relevant since most MLIPs are message-passing GNNs. Founded in 2022 (originally virtual). LoG 2026 is the fifth overall and second in-person edition, November 20-22, 2026, at Northeastern University, Boston. Verified from the official site.

benchmarks.name: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
benchmarks.description: Long-established general AI conference promoting theoretical and applied AI research; carries a growing AI-for-science track relevant to molecular property prediction. The next edition listed on the official site is the Forty-first AAAI Conference, February 16-23, 2027, in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Verified from the official site (note: the site listed 2027 as the upcoming edition at time of checking).

benchmarks.name: KDD — ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
benchmarks.description: The premier data mining and data science conference, run by ACM's Special Interest Group on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining; hosts applied-science tracks and materials-informatics work. KDD 2026 runs August 9-13, 2026 in Jeju, Korea. Verified from the official SIGKDD site.

benchmarks.name: MLDD — Machine Learning for Drug Discovery Workshop (ICLR)
benchmarks.description: ICLR workshop focused on machine learning for drug discovery, covering molecular representation, generative chemistry, docking and binding-affinity prediction. Adjacent to but distinct from the MLIP community, and a common venue for molecular property prediction papers.

benchmarks.name: ML4LMS — Machine Learning for Life and Material Sciences Workshop (ICML)
benchmarks.description: ICML workshop bridging ML methods with life sciences and materials science applications, emphasizing benchmarks, datasets and industrial relevance.

benchmarks.name: Psi-k Network and Psi-k Conference
benchmarks.description: Europe-based international network for first-principles computational materials science, established in 1994, developing theory, algorithms and codes to predict material properties. Organized bottom-up via a Board of Trustees, Scientific Advisory Committee and 22 Working Groups; sponsors roughly 20-25 workshops, conferences, schools and tutorials annually, an annual research conference jointly with CECAM, and a full-field conference every few years. Maintains a 2,000+ member mailing list and publishes newsletters. Verified from psi-k.net.

benchmarks.name: CECAM — Centre Européen de Calcul Atomique et Moléculaire
benchmarks.description: Headquartered at EPFL Lausanne, CECAM promotes fundamental research on advanced computational methods for atomistic and molecular simulation, now spanning materials science, biology and medicinal chemistry. Runs flagship workshops (including deep learning in materials science), hands-on schools, and research conferences, plus CECAM Lectures, CECAM-Marvel Classics, the Mansigh Conversation Series and the Berni J. Alder Prize. Scope and activities verified from cecam.org; the 1969 founding year is from background knowledge and was not confirmed on the fetched page.

benchmarks.name: CECAM MLIP Schools / Hands-on Machine Learning Potentials Workshops
benchmarks.description: Recurring CECAM hands-on schools and flagship workshops teaching machine-learning interatomic potentials — training GAP/ACE/NequIP/MACE, active learning, and running MD with learned potentials. These are the standard European training route for new MLIP PhD students and are announced via the CECAM events calendar and the Psi-k mailing list.

benchmarks.name: IPAM — Institute for Pure & Applied Mathematics (UCLA) Long Programs
benchmarks.description: NSF Mathematical Sciences Institute at UCLA whose mission is to foster interaction of mathematics with science and technology and build interdisciplinary research communities. Its multi-month Long Programs have repeatedly convened the ML-for-chemistry/materials community and produced durable public lecture recordings. Verified that IPAM runs long programs and workshops from ipam.ucla.edu; the homepage did not enumerate a current MLIP-specific long program, and the 2000 founding year is background knowledge, not confirmed on the fetched page.

benchmarks.name: Gordon Research Conference — Computational Chemistry
benchmarks.description: Biennial off-the-record Gordon Research Conference on computational chemistry covering theoretical methods, molecular simulation, data science, quantum computing and AI-driven molecular discovery. Held every 24 months since its inception in 1986. The 2026 meeting runs July 19-24, 2026 at the Hotel Rey Don Jaime in Spain, themed 'Molecular Discovery and Simulation in the AI Era'. Verified from grc.org.

benchmarks.name: Gordon Research Conference — Machine Learning (and associated GRS)
benchmarks.description: Gordon Research Conferences run ML-focused meetings and Gordon Research Seminars (student/postdoc-run precursor days) touching chemistry and materials applications. The GRC format — no proceedings, unpublished work, small attendance — makes these unusually good for seeing MLIP results a year before preprint.

benchmarks.name: MRS Fall and Spring Meetings (Materials Research Society)
benchmarks.description: The Materials Research Society runs the twice-yearly MRS Spring and Fall Meetings, the largest general materials conferences, each with multiple symposia dedicated to AI/ML for materials and to machine-learning interatomic potentials. MRS Fall (traditionally Boston) is also where the e3nn team gave its widely used 2021 tutorial.

benchmarks.name: APS March Meeting
benchmarks.description: The American Physical Society's March Meeting is the largest annual physics conference and a major venue for condensed-matter and computational-materials work, with dedicated sessions on machine learning for electronic structure and interatomic potentials.

benchmarks.name: ACS Spring and Fall National Meetings
benchmarks.description: The American Chemical Society's twice-yearly national meetings, with the COMP (Computers in Chemistry) and CINF (Chemical Information) divisions hosting substantial ML-for-chemistry programming including machine-learned force fields and molecular property prediction. NOTE: acs.org returned HTTP 403 to my fetch and no search was available, so upcoming dates, locations and a verified URL could not be confirmed.

benchmarks.name: TMS Annual Meeting & Exhibition
benchmarks.description: The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society annual meeting, with growing symposia on AI/ML in materials design, ICME (Integrated Computational Materials Engineering) and machine-learned potentials for alloys.

benchmarks.name: Faraday Discussions (Royal Society of Chemistry)
benchmarks.description: Distinctive RSC meeting format in which papers are circulated in advance and the recorded discussion is published alongside them; several volumes have been devoted to machine learning in molecular simulation and materials chemistry, making them unusually candid records of community disagreement.

benchmarks.name: MLST — Machine Learning: Science and Technology (IOP)
benchmarks.description: Open-access IOP Publishing journal (ISSN 2632-2153) dedicated to machine learning across the sciences, and one of the most common homes for MLIP methods and benchmarking papers that sit between an ML conference and a chemistry journal. NOTE: iopscience.iop.org returned HTTP 403 to my fetch and the search budget was exhausted, so the founding year and URL are from background knowledge and should be re-verified.

benchmarks.name: npj Computational Materials
benchmarks.description: Nature Portfolio open-access journal for computational materials science; the primary journal venue for MLIP papers aimed at the materials community (CHGNet, M3GNet, ACE variants, and the Ko & Ong MLIP review all appeared here).

benchmarks.name: Nature Machine Intelligence
benchmarks.description: Nature Portfolio journal covering machine learning and AI including applications to the physical sciences; publishes high-profile molecular ML and foundation-model-for-chemistry papers.

benchmarks.name: Nature Computational Science
benchmarks.description: Nature Portfolio journal for computational methods and their application across disciplines, including atomistic simulation and machine-learned potentials.

benchmarks.name: Digital Discovery (RSC)
benchmarks.description: Royal Society of Chemistry open-access journal for data science, ML and automation in chemistry and materials; notable for accepting datasets, software and negative results alongside methods papers.

benchmarks.name: The Journal of Chemical Physics (AIP)
benchmarks.description: AIP Publishing's flagship chemical physics journal and the historical home of neural-network potential work — Behler-Parrinello symmetry functions and much of the first- and second-generation HDNNP literature. Runs special topics issues on machine learning in chemical physics.

benchmarks.name: JCTC — Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation (ACS)
benchmarks.description: ACS journal for theoretical and computational chemistry methods; a standard venue for force-field development, MLIP benchmarking against high-level theory, and free-energy/MD methodology.

benchmarks.name: JCIM — Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling (ACS)
benchmarks.description: ACS journal covering cheminformatics, molecular representation and property prediction; the classic venue for QSAR-lineage and molecular-descriptor work that underpins modern molecular property prediction benchmarks. Chem. Doc., later renamed) from background knowledge.

benchmarks.name: Behler 2021 — Four Generations of High-Dimensional Neural Network Potentials
benchmarks.description: Jörg Behler's Chemical Reviews review organizing the entire neural-network-potential field into four generations, from early low-dimensional fits through Behler-Parrinello HDNNPs to charge- and long-range-aware fourth-generation models. The standard orienting read for any new MLIP PhD student and the source of the 'generations' vocabulary the field now uses.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Four Generations of High-Dimensional Neural Network Potentials
benchmarks.creators: Jörg Behler

benchmarks.name: Musil et al. 2021 — Physics-Inspired Structural Representations for Molecules and Materials
benchmarks.description: Chemical Reviews review examining how atomic structures are converted into mathematical representations for ML in chemistry and materials, exploring 'the link between properties, structures, their physical chemistry and their mathematical description'. The definitive treatment of the descriptor/representation layer (SOAP, ACE, symmetry functions) and their formal relationships. Submitted 12 Jan 2021, final version 4 Aug 2021; DOI 10.1021/acs.chemrev.1c00021. Verified via the arXiv record.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Physics-inspired structural representations for molecules and materials
benchmarks.creators: Felix Musil, Andrea Grisafi, Albert P. Bartók, Christoph Ortner, Gábor Csányi, Michele Ceriotti

benchmarks.name: Unke et al. 2021 — Machine Learning Force Fields
benchmarks.description: Comprehensive Chemical Reviews review of machine learning force fields covering kernel and neural approaches, descriptors, training data generation, and practical deployment in MD. Published in Chem. Rev. 2021, 121(16), 10142-10186; first posted to arXiv 14 Oct 2020 (revised 12 Jan 2021), so the first-public year is 2020. Together with Behler 2021 and Musil 2021 it forms the standard three-review foundation for the field. Verified via the arXiv record.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Machine Learning Force Fields
benchmarks.creators: Oliver T. Unke, Stefan Chmiela, Huziel E. Sauceda, Michael Gastegger, Igor Poltavsky, Kristof T. Schütt, Alexandre Tkatchenko, Klaus-Robert Müller

benchmarks.name: Batatia et al. — The Design Space of E(3)-Equivariant Atom-Centered Interatomic Potentials
benchmarks.description: Unifying theory paper connecting ACE and NequIP: it generalizes the Atomic Cluster Expansion so it 'can be recast as one layer of a multi-layer architecture', then systematically ablates design choices against accuracy and extrapolation behavior. Introduces BOTNet, 'a much-simplified version of NequIP' that matches benchmark performance while being more interpretable. Essential reading for understanding why MACE is built the way it is. Submitted 13 May 2022, revised 24 Nov 2022. Verified via the arXiv record.
benchmarks.paperTitle: The Design Space of E(3)-Equivariant Atom-Centered Interatomic Potentials
benchmarks.creators: Ilyes Batatia, Simon Batzner, Dávid Péter Kovács, Albert Musaelian, Gregor N. C. Simm, Ralf Drautz, Christoph Ortner, Boris Kozinsky, Gábor Csányi

benchmarks.description: The Deringer/Csányi review lineage (including 'Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials as Emerging Tools for Materials Science', Adv. Mater. 2019, and the later Chem. Rev. treatment of Gaussian Process Regression / GAP for materials) is the standard entry point for the kernel-based branch of MLIPs and for how GAP is actually fit and validated in practice.

benchmarks.name: e3nn — Euclidean Neural Networks Framework and Tutorials
benchmarks.description: 'A modular PyTorch framework for Euclidean neural networks' providing the E(3)-equivariant building blocks (irreps, tensor products, spherical harmonics) underlying NequIP, Allegro and MACE. Two implementations exist: e3nn-torch and e3nn-jax. Core developers are Mario Geiger (project lead) and Tess Smidt. Ships Jupyter-notebook tutorials, the widely used MRS 2021 Fall Meeting Tutorial, recommended group-theory/representation-theory reading, recorded 2019-2020 talks, a Slack channel and GitHub discussions. These docs plus the notebook tutorials are the practical route to understanding irreps and equivariant tensor products before reading the NequIP/MACE papers. Both URLs were verified as appearing on the fetched e3nn.org page.

benchmarks.name: MolSSI — The Molecular Sciences Software Institute
benchmarks.description: Describes itself as 'a nexus for science, education, and cooperation for the global computational molecular sciences community', building open-source infrastructure and running education across computational chemistry, materials science and biomolecular simulation. Runs Software Fellowships for graduate students and postdocs, the ACT-CMS curricular program, online credentialed courses, community workshops (accelerated computing, quantum chemistry, AI-assisted development) and best-practices software training.

benchmarks.name: matsci.org — Materials Science Community Discourse
benchmarks.description: The main community forum for computational materials science, self-described as 'Community discussion for materials science and support for common scientific codes and databases', co-managed by the Materials Project and the KIM Project. benchmarks.name: Atom-Density Representations
benchmarks.description: Recasts atomic-structure representations in an abstract, basis-independent bra-ket notation built on a smoothed atom density plus Haar integration over the symmetry group. This makes explicit that SOAP power spectra, Behler-Parrinello symmetry functions, N-body kernels, and tensorial SOAP are all special cases of one construction differing only in basis and symmetrization choices. The formalism also enables alchemical/chemical-space compression, and it is the conceptual scaffold on which NICE and later equivariant work is built. Preprint 2018; published JCP 2019.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Atom-density representations for machine learning
benchmarks.creators: Michael J. Willatt, Félix Musil, Michele Ceriotti

benchmarks.name: ACE: Completeness, Efficiency and Stability
benchmarks.description: Supplies the mathematical framework for systematically deriving polynomial bases that are invariant to isometry and permutation, with a precomputation algorithm that guarantees the resulting basis is genuinely complete rather than merely plausible. It also gives a fast recursive evaluation scheme and analyses numerical stability. This paper is what turned ACE from an elegant expansion into a rigorously certified, production-grade approximation scheme, and it underpins ACE1.jl/ACEpotentials.jl. Preprint 2019; published J. Comput. Phys. 2022.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Atomic cluster expansion: Completeness, efficiency and stability
benchmarks.creators: Geneviève Dusson, Markus Bachmayr, Gábor Csányi, Ralf Drautz, Simon Etter, Cas van der Oord, Christoph Ortner

benchmarks.name: Physics-Inspired Structural Representations
benchmarks.description: The authoritative review of how Cartesian coordinates are transformed into representations for atomistic ML, written jointly by the SOAP, ACE, and Ceriotti-group lineages. Its lasting value is showing the deep structural connections between frameworks that look unrelated on the surface — symmetry functions, SOAP, bispectrum, ACE, and kernel methods — as choices within a shared density-expansion-plus-symmetrization construction. This is the standard orientation text for anyone entering the density branch.
benchmarks.paperTitle: Physics-Inspired Structural Representations for Molecules and Materials
benchmarks.creators: Félix Musil, Andrea Grisafi, Albert P. Bartók, Christoph Ortner, Gábor Csányi, Michele Ceriotti

benchmarks.name: Neural scaling of deep chemical models
benchmarks.description: This is the foundational scaling-law paper for the atomistic/chemical domain, deliberately spanning both branches: generative chemical language models (ChemGPT, >1B parameters) and GNN-based machine-learned interatomic potentials, varied over orders of magnitude in model and dataset size. It fits empirical neural-scaling relations (exponent ~0.17 for chemical LMs at the largest dataset size) and asks the field's central open question — whether physical priors help or hinder as you scale. It set up the scaling-vs-symmetry debate that EScAIP, Orb, PET and AllScAIP later fought out.

roadmap.summary: State of the field, mid-2026: the "universal MLIP" era is now firmly post-hype. Foundation models (UMA, MACE-MP/OMAT, eSEN, GRACE, SevenNet, MatterSim) are commodities — Matbench Discovery lists 41 models, the top ~5 are separated by ~0.02 CPS, and MLIP Studio (arXiv:2607.07606) now serves 60+ of them from one web UI. That compression is the single most important strategic fact for a PhD student: architecture-chasing on energy/force MAE is a losing bet. The differentiating work has moved to (a) physics the short-range GNN ansatz structurally cannot represent — long-range electrostatics, charge transfer, spin, electronic entropy, excited states; (b) honesty about error — UQ that includes inherited DFT error, not just ensemble spread; and (c) whether any of it survives contact with a real simulation, where benchmarks are now exposing embarrassing gaps (pressure poorly described across most foundation models per Dyna-Mat arXiv:2607.03433; amorphous phases broken per Deringer arXiv:2607.11384; sophisticated models delivering 3-5 meV/atom for near-DFT wall-clock per arXiv:2607.07647).

openProblems.title: DFT-error inheritance and anchoring MLIPs to experiment
openProblems.description: Every MLIP inherits the systematic error of its reference functional, but standard UQ (ensembles, evidential, Bayesian) reports only spread relative to that functional — it is silent on the fact that the functional itself is wrong. A model can be perfectly confident and perfectly wrong. The frontier is multi-fidelity training across several electronic-structure references plus calibration against experimental observables (cohesive/atomization energies, lattice constants, bulk moduli), so uncertainty reflects distance from reality rather than distance from PBE. Kellner, Ceriotti, Jacobsen et al. (PET-UAFD / PET-EXP) is the landmark statement of the problem and the first credible answer.
openProblems.whyHard: Requires jointly handling functional disagreement, sparse and heterogeneous experimental data with its own error bars, and finite-temperature/anharmonic/nuclear-quantum corrections needed to compare a 0 K calculation to a room-temperature measurement. It is also thankless: it makes your numbers look worse, not better, so incentives run against it. Demands genuine fluency in both ML and experimental condensed-matter metrology — a rare combination, which is exactly the moat.

openProblems.title: Magnetism, spin degrees of freedom, and electronic entropy
openProblems.description: Mainstream MLIPs map geometry to energy and have no spin coordinate at all, so they cannot represent magnetic configuration energetics, spin-lattice coupling, or the mixed-valence/charge-state physics central to Fe/Co/Ni alloys, battery cathodes, and correlated oxides. Foundation models fail here specifically and reproducibly: an 80-model catalysis benchmark (arXiv:2512.16702) found magnetic materials to be a distinct failure mode, and arXiv:2607.08351 found foundation MLIPs capture geometric ordering in perovskite oxides but miss purely local multiplet population shifts. Work is fragmenting into spin-explicit potentials (spin-MLIP/MTP, magnetic HIP-NN), magnetic-moment-aware fine-tuning, and electronic-entropy/charge-state representations.
openProblems.whyHard: Spin-polarized DFT reference data is expensive, and constrained/soft-constrained spin-polarized DFT is needed to sample non-ground-state magnetic configurations — a specialist skill in itself. The magnetic state is partly an independent dynamical variable, not a function of geometry, so the standard equivariant ansatz is structurally inadequate rather than merely undertrained. Collinear vs. non-collinear is a further cliff: almost all current work is collinear, and non-collinear is largely untouched. There is also no accepted benchmark, so progress is hard to measure.

openProblems.title: Excited states, nonadiabatic dynamics, and photochemistry
openProblems.description: Nearly the entire MLIP field learns a single ground-state PES. Photochemistry needs multiple coupled surfaces, nonadiabatic couplings, and correct topology at conical intersections — where the Born-Oppenheimer surfaces become degenerate and the adiabatic representation is singular. X-MACE (arXiv:2604.12699) is the standout: transferable multi-surface excited-state dynamics good enough to screen fluorescent protein chromophores, which is the first time excited-state MLIPs have looked like a screening tool rather than a per-molecule craft project. FieldMACE adds multipole long-range coupling for ground and excited states.
openProblems.whyHard: Nonadiabatic couplings carry an arbitrary sign/phase that is not a smooth function of geometry, so naive regression is ill-posed — you must either learn a phaseless object or work in a diabatic representation that is itself not uniquely defined. Conical intersections are non-smooth by construction, defeating the smoothness priors that make MLIPs work. Reference data requires multireference quantum chemistry (CASSCF/CASPT2/MRCI), which is expensive, hard to automate, and hard to converge consistently across a dataset — so training sets are tiny and transferability is largely unestablished. Very few people can do both the multireference chemistry and the ML.

openProblems.title: Amorphous and disordered phases: the transferability wall
openProblems.description: Universal MLIPs are trained overwhelmingly on relaxed or near-equilibrium crystalline structures (Materials Project lineage), and they degrade badly on glasses, amorphous films, and disordered networks — precisely the systems driving phase-change memory, amorphous oxide semiconductors, and battery interphases. Deringer's group has made this a named frontier challenge with a curated benchmark over canonical amorphous systems. The medium-range-order result is the sharpest version: arXiv:2604.21222 uses neutron/X-ray diffraction to show that even long-range MLIP extensions fail to reproduce medium-range order in silica glass — i.e. the failure is not fixed by adding Ewald.
openProblems.whyHard: Amorphous structure is defined by a distribution over configurations, not a single minimum, so validation requires matching experimental structure factors and ring statistics rather than energies — a different and harder success criterion. Generating reference data requires melt-quench trajectories at DFT cost, and the physically relevant quench rates are many orders of magnitude slower than anything simulable, so there is an irreducible protocol-dependence. Medium-range order (5-15 Angstrom) sits in a gap between what local descriptors capture and what electrostatics fixes, and nobody currently knows what representation closes it.

openProblems.title: Efficiency, MD throughput, and the accuracy-cost Pareto front
openProblems.description: The field optimizes energy/force MAE and reports it on A100-class hardware, but the deliverable is nanoseconds of MD on the hardware a real lab owns. A benchmark of 23 mainstream models on a 192-atom system under lab-realistic constraints (Kang, Lu, Meng, Liu) found that sophisticated models buy only 3-5 meV/atom while degrading throughput so severely that in extreme cases they run barely faster than the DFT they were meant to replace — and concluded that accuracy-only benchmarking 'misleads the field'. The counter-movement is distillation and compression: SevenNet-Nano (order-of-magnitude speedup), structural pruning (1.5-4x), message-passing pruning + graph partitioning for million-atom runs, and model merging (GFFMERGE, 5-27x).
openProblems.whyHard: Equivariant tensor products are the accuracy engine and the cost center simultaneously, so compression fights the inductive bias that makes the models work. Message passing couples throughput to graph topology and to the parallel decomposition, so speedups do not survive going multi-GPU or multi-node without real systems engineering. The deeper problem is sociological: efficiency papers are read as engineering rather than science and get cited less, so the Pareto front stays underexplored despite everyone needing it. Publishing here requires credible hardware benchmarking, which most ML groups are not set up to do rigorously.

openProblems.title: End-to-end observable benchmarking: does the simulation actually work?
openProblems.description: Force MAE is a proxy that has decoupled from the thing we care about. The 2025-26 wave of end-to-end benchmarks is systematically finding that models which look near-identical on leaderboards diverge badly on real observables. Dyna-Mat (arXiv:2607.03433) benchmarks against first-principles MD trajectories and finds pressure remains poorly described across most foundation models — a devastating result for anything NPT, i.e. most materials science. Matbench Discovery has responded by adding a (self-described 'preliminary') MD leaderboard scoring RDFs and vibrational DOS, and weighting thermal conductivity (kSRME) at 40% of its composite score. MOF chemistry at high temperature (arXiv:2604.25262), alkali-ion battery kinetics (arXiv:2601.10938), and lunar regolith minerals (arXiv:2607.09005) all show large errors invisible to standard metrics.
openProblems.whyHard: Reference data means long ab initio MD trajectories, which is exactly the cost you adopted MLIPs to avoid — so ground truth is scarce by construction. Observables like pressure, thermal conductivity, and free energies are sensitive to systematic error in ways forces are not, and they entangle model error with simulation protocol (thermostat, timestep, finite size, sampling), making attribution genuinely difficult. Benchmarks are also a public good with private cost: they take enormous effort, embarrass powerful groups, and are cited as infrastructure rather than as discovery.

openProblems.title: Long-range electrostatics, charge transfer, and polarization
openProblems.description: The classic structural limitation: a finite-cutoff GNN cannot represent Coulomb interactions, so short-range MLIPs produce qualitatively wrong physics — spurious metallization at polar interfaces (arXiv:2603.04228), no LO-TO splitting, no dielectric response, no charge transfer. This has moved fastest of any problem on this list. Kim & Cheng's Latent Ewald Summation perspective (arXiv:2512.18029) argues the recipe is now simple and universal: use a Coulomb functional form with environment-dependent charges and do NOT train on ambiguous DFT partial charges. MACE-POLAR-1 (Batatia, Csányi et al., trained on 100M hybrid-DFT calculations) delivers polarizable induction and charge equilibration with learnable Fukui functions at sub-kcal/mol molecular crystal formation energies. Approaches now include reciprocal-space equivariance (EquiEwald), differentiable PME, attention in reciprocal space, PSWF expansions, and charge-aware NEP (qNEP).
openProblems.whyHard: Partial charges are not quantum observables — every partition scheme (Hirshfeld, Bader, DDAP) disagrees, so supervising on them bakes in an arbitrary convention; the field's fix is to learn latent charges from energies alone, which is elegant but weakly constrained. Self-consistent charge equilibration adds an inner solve inside every MD step, hurting throughput and complicating gradients. Charge transfer under bond breaking and global charge conservation across fragments remain genuinely unsolved (arXiv:2604.27910). And crucially, long-range is necessary but not sufficient: silica medium-range order still fails.

openProblems.title: Uncertainty quantification and active learning
openProblems.description: UQ is the backbone of active learning and of trusting MLIP-driven MD, and it has matured fast: shallow/multi-head committees give cheap ensembles on foundation models (arXiv:2508.09907), Bayesian equivariant potentials scale (arXiv:2510.03046), calibration frameworks give order-of-magnitude improvements in uncertainty-error correlation (arXiv:2510.00721), and the acquisition-function literature is now rich (neural tangent kernels, determinantal point processes, entropy maximization, pretrained-representation signals, Stein kernelized MD). The genuinely interesting recent turn is propagating uncertainty to observables rather than reporting it on forces — Girsanov reweighting for rare-event kinetics (arXiv:2607.13757) pushes MLIP uncertainty through to committor probabilities and rate constants.
openProblems.whyHard: Ensembles are the only thing that reliably works and they cost Nx inference, which is unaffordable for foundation-scale models — hence the scramble for single-model UQ that is honest. Calibration on an i.i.d. test split says nothing about the out-of-distribution regime where you actually need it, which is the whole point. Propagating a per-force error bar through a chaotic trajectory to a free energy or a rate is a hard stochastic-analysis problem, not a plotting exercise. And, as the DFT-inheritance entry notes, all of this is uncertainty relative to a functional that is itself biased — most of the literature quietly ignores this.

openProblems.title: Reactive chemistry, rare events, and electrochemical interfaces
openProblems.description: Foundation models are trained near equilibrium and see almost no transition states, so barriers — the quantity that determines every rate — are the least reliable thing they predict. The productive direction is targeted active learning in barrier regions: transition-path-sampling-based active learning discovering electrochemical mechanisms (arXiv:2605.03737), pretrained latent spaces as acquisition signals specifically for reactive chemistry (arXiv:2605.03964), and ML-predicted Hessian eigenvectors for transition-state finding with UQ-based failure detection (arXiv:2603.21323). Electrochemical interfaces are the hardest instance because they need reactivity, charge transfer, and applied potential simultaneously; hybrid schemes (QM/ML, PFP/MM, mixture-of-experts partitioning reactive interfaces from bulk) are a pragmatic hedge.
openProblems.whyHard: Transition states are measure-zero in equilibrium sampling — you cannot get them by running MD, so data generation requires enhanced sampling that itself needs a potential, a chicken-and-egg loop. Barriers are exponentially amplified in rates, so meV-scale energy error becomes order-of-magnitude rate error, an accuracy demand far beyond what leaderboards certify. Reactive systems change bonding topology and charge state, breaking both fixed-charge schemes and the near-equilibrium training distribution at once. At electrodes you additionally need grand-canonical electron treatment, which sits outside standard MLIP formalism entirely.

openProblems.title: Phonons, thermal transport, and anharmonicity
openProblems.description: Thermal conductivity is now a first-class MLIP metric — Matbench Discovery weights kSRME at 40% of its composite score, which single-handedly redirected a chunk of the field. This is a rare case of a benchmark successfully forcing models to respect physics beyond forces, since kSRME punishes errors in third-order force constants that energy MAE never sees. Infrastructure has matured (kALDo 2.0, cepstral analysis for Green-Kubo in MOFs), and application work is prolific: superionic conductors, interfacial conductance, thermal transistors, ultralow-kappa screening. A dedicated phonon benchmark of foundation models exists (arXiv:2509.03401).
openProblems.whyHard: Thermal conductivity depends on third- and fourth-order derivatives of the PES, so it is exquisitely sensitive to smoothness and to error the training loss never penalized — a model can nail forces and produce nonsense phonons. Strongly anharmonic, superionic, and disordered systems break the perturbative phonon picture entirely, requiring Green-Kubo or Wigner-transport treatments with long trajectories and heavy statistics. Heat-flux definitions for many-body message-passing potentials are subtle and were historically implemented wrongly. As a research direction it is now partly a victim of its own benchmark success: the metric exists, models are optimizing it, and marginal papers are getting harder to distinguish.

openProblems.title: Foundation-model fine-tuning and data efficiency
openProblems.description: The dominant practical workflow of 2026: take UMA/MACE-OMAT/eSEN, fine-tune on tens to hundreds of targeted DFT points, run production MD. Results are strong and reproducible — barocaloric phase transitions from 5-10 DFT configurations (arXiv:2606.25742), force predictions improved 5-15x across architectures by fine-tuning (arXiv:2511.05337), CCSD(T)-accuracy non-covalent interactions with 60% less high-fidelity data via physics-informed distillation (arXiv:2606.05127). Sub-directions: optimizer choice (AdamW/ScheduleFree beat Adam; SOAP/Muon under partial force supervision), sparsity-promoting/parameter-efficient adaptation, universal models as configuration-space generators for DFT relabeling, and label-efficient training.
openProblems.whyHard: The mechanics are easy, which is exactly the problem — this is where everyone is, so novelty is scarce and papers increasingly read as 'we fine-tuned MACE on our system'. The real open questions are less glamorous: catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning narrow, no principled way to know how much data a given system needs before spending the DFT, and no theory of which pretraining distribution transfers to which target. Distillation and merging fight the same tension. A student entering here needs a genuinely novel system or a methodological insight, not a fine-tuning run.

openProblems.title: Architecture design for equivariant potentials
openProblems.description: The perennial engine room: higher-order equivariant message passing, attention mechanisms, Cartesian vs. spherical tensor formulations, Clebsch-Gordan-free approaches. 2026 entrants include edge cluster expansion with radial rotary attention (arXiv:2607.10664), all-to-all node attention for long-range (arXiv:2603.06567), and TACE's spectral/spatial tensor cluster expansion (arXiv:2509.14961). Matbench Discovery's top five models sit within roughly 0.02 CPS of one another — EquiformerV3+DeNS-OAM, TECE-OAM-RRA, EquFlashV2, GRACE-3L-OAM-L, eSEN-30M-OAM — which is the clearest possible signal that architecture is no longer the binding constraint.
openProblems.whyHard: Not hard so much as saturated: gains are now within benchmark noise and increasingly attributable to data (the OAM/OMat pretraining corpus) rather than architecture, so attribution of any claimed improvement is genuinely ambiguous. Competing here means competing with Meta FAIR, Microsoft, and Cambridge on compute and data you do not have. The accuracy-cost benchmark (arXiv:2607.07647) further suggests recent architectural sophistication has negative practical value once throughput is priced in. A student should treat architectures as tools to be used, not targets to be beaten — unless attacking a representational gap (spin, excited states, charge) that no amount of data fixes.

openProblems.title: Differentiable simulation and inverse design
openProblems.description: Making the whole simulation — not just the energy model — differentiable, so you can backpropagate from a macroscopic observable or a design target to potential parameters or to structure. Live threads: differentiable particle-mesh Ewald with Cartesian tensor message passing (arXiv:2606.01598), differentiable hybrid force fields for autonomous electrolyte discovery (arXiv:2604.07979), differentiable OPLS parameterization applied to 10,000+ electrolyte formulations (arXiv:2607.04633), opt-DDAP charges via autodiff (arXiv:2604.10984), implicit differentiation through relaxed structures (arXiv:2407.02414), and GNN simulators with differentiability for inverse materials design (arXiv:2605.09495). Inverse design of bespoke potentials by information-matching (arXiv:2606.08148) is a nice conceptual entry.
openProblems.whyHard: Backpropagating through thousands of MD steps explodes or vanishes gradients and blows up memory; chaos means the true gradient of a long-trajectory observable can be meaningless even when computable. Implicit differentiation and adjoint methods help but require care and are not plug-and-play. Tooling is fragmented — the differentiable-simulation story is natural in JAX (JAX-MD) while the model ecosystem consolidated on PyTorch, so practitioners pay an integration tax; torch-sim is partially closing this. The direction is genuinely promising and genuinely underpopulated, but demands unusual comfort with both numerical analysis and ML engineering.

openProblems.title: Agentic and LLM-driven MLIP development
openProblems.description: A fast-emerging 2026 thread: LLM agents automating the MLIP lifecycle end-to-end. Lang2MLIP (arXiv:2605.14527) goes from natural-language spec to trained potential via autonomous multi-agent workflows; MLIPilot (arXiv:2605.30889) has LLM agents optimize training strategy under constrained domain validation; AtomisticSkills (arXiv:2605.24002) packages 100+ DFT/MLIP skills for agentic research; and a solid-electrolyte perspective (arXiv:2606.24480) frames MLIP+LLM as the discovery loop. Worth watching, and worth a healthy skepticism.
openProblems.whyHard: Validation is the whole problem: an agent that produces a plausible-looking potential which is subtly wrong is worse than no potential, and the field's own benchmarks (see the end-to-end entry) show that even human experts routinely ship models with broken pressure or phonons. So agentic MLIP development inherits an evaluation crisis it cannot itself resolve, and current papers lean heavily on demonstrations rather than rigorous head-to-head against expert-built potentials. Nascent and hype-adjacent — genuine opportunity for someone who takes verification seriously, a trap for someone who does not.

groups: Various — this space is too new to have settled leaders

stack.name: fairchem (Meta FAIR Chemistry)
stack.role: Highest-priority to learn. Centralized home for UMA foundation models (uma-s-1p2 fastest/SOTA, uma-m-1p1 best-in-class) with task-conditioned heads for oc20/oc22/oc25 catalysis, omat inorganic, omol molecules/polymers, odac MOFs, omc molecular crystals. Note v2 is a breaking change incompatible with v1 checkpoints; core 2.21.0 as of June 2026, ~quarterly release cadence. Whatever you build will be benchmarked against this.

stack.name: mace-torch (ACEsuit/MACE)
stack.role: The academic counterweight to fairchem and the most fine-tuned-upon codebase in the literature. Higher-order equivariant message passing. Ships MACE-MP-0 (s/m/l, 89 elements), MACE-MP-0b3, MACE-MPA-0, MACE-OMAT-0, MACE-MATPES (PBE and r2SCAN), MACE-OFF23 for organics, MACE-OMOL-0, MACE-MH-0/1, and PolarMACE checkpoints. v0.3.16 (May 2026), MIT. If you fine-tune anything in a paper, it will probably be this.

stack.name: torch-sim
stack.role: The most important recent addition to the stack and the one most students are sleeping on. GPU-native batched simulation engine 'for the MLIP era' — up to 100x over ASE, with automatic memory management, NVE/NVT/NPT Langevin integrators, relaxation, swap Monte Carlo. Model-agnostic across MACE, fairchem, SevenNet, ORB, MatterSim; integrates ASE/pymatgen/phonopy. v0.6.0 (April 2026), MIT. Learn this if you care about throughput.

stack.name: e3nn
stack.role: Foundational library for E(3)-equivariant networks — tensor products, spherical harmonics, irreps bookkeeping. You do not need to write e3nn to use MACE/NequIP, but you must be able to read it to modify architectures or to add a new equivariant output head (dipoles, Born charges, spin). Collaborative output of LBNL/EPFL/FU Berlin; Tess Smidt's lineage.

stack.name: ASE (Atomic Simulation Environment)
stack.role: The lingua franca — Atoms objects, calculators, I/O, basic MD/optimizers, DFT-code interfaces. Non-negotiable baseline literacy; every MLIP ships an ASE calculator. But understand its limits: it is Python-loop-bound and is now the throughput bottleneck that torch-sim exists to replace. Use it for glue and prototyping, not production MD. Note the project lives on GitLab, not GitHub. GPLv2+.

stack.name: LAMMPS
stack.role: The production MD workhorse for large-scale/parallel materials simulation from Sandia; ~50k commits, C++, GPLv2. Where you go for million-atom runs, fracture, radiation damage, long trajectories on HPC. MLIP interfaces exist via pair styles (pair_style mace/allegro/nep etc.) though the front page I fetched does not advertise ML support — check the pair_style docs at lammps.org. Essential if your PhD touches mechanical or defect properties.

stack.name: GPUMD / NEP
stack.role: Underrated and highly strategic. Fully GPU-implemented general-purpose MD (CUDA 68%), home of the neuroevolution potential (NEP) family. The throughput-first design philosophy — deliberately cheaper models, enormous trajectories — is the natural home for thermal transport, and it is where much of the kappa literature and the charge-aware qNEP work happens. Requires CUDA cc>=3.5. If you do thermal conductivity, learn this, not just MACE.

stack.name: i-PI
stack.role: Python force-engine server implementing advanced sampling, with the electronic-structure or MLIP code as a client. The standard tool for path-integral MD and nuclear quantum effects — which matter more than most people admit for anything with hydrogen, and for water in particular. Also carries a UQ framework designed for use with MLIPs (arXiv:2405.15224). Learn it if you touch NQE, isotope effects, or free energies.

stack.name: JAX-MD
stack.role: Accelerated differentiable MD — XLA-compiled, runs CPU/GPU/TPU, autodiff throughout. Alive but niche now: v0.2.29 (June 2026), 12 releases, self-described 'under development'. The ecosystem consolidated on PyTorch, so choose JAX-MD deliberately — it is the right call for differentiable-simulation and inverse-design research (see that open problem), and the wrong call if you mainly want to use foundation models.

stack.name: MLIP Studio
stack.role: Free interactive web platform unifying 60+ universal MLIPs for property prediction, geometry optimization, vibrational and EOS analysis, and high-throughput benchmarking. Not a research skill so much as a reconnaissance tool — the fastest way to sanity-check how a dozen foundation models behave on your system before committing to one. Its existence is itself evidence of how commoditized universal MLIPs have become.

stack.name: Matbench Discovery
stack.role: The scoreboard you must be able to read critically. 41 models ranked by CPS = 50% discovery F1 + 40% thermal conductivity kSRME + 10% geometry RMSD. Top-5 clustered within ~0.02 CPS (EquiformerV3+DeNS-OAM, TECE-OAM-RRA-1.0, EquFlashV2, GRACE-3L-OAM-L, eSEN-30M-OAM). Recently added a preliminary MD leaderboard scoring RDFs and vibrational DOS. Caveat worth internalizing: stability evaluation uses DFT reference energies rather than model predictions, which differs from other benchmarks.

stack.name: kALDo
stack.role: Open-source anharmonic lattice dynamics / thermal transport package, v2.0 (Feb 2026), built to consume MLIPs directly. Scales to crystals and disordered materials. The practical entry point if you work on phonons or kappa — pair with phonopy for harmonic properties and GPUMD for Green-Kubo.

stack.name: OpenMM
stack.role: Biomolecular MD engine, relevant if your work drifts toward proteins/drug discovery (see MACE-OFF, MACE-OMOL, implicit-solvent MLIPs like arXiv:2607.10887, and MACE-POLAR-1's protein-ligand claims). The openmm-ml bridge lets you swap in ML potentials for a QM region. I could not verify a canonical URL within this session's fetch budget, so I have left it blank rather than guess — it is easily found and this omission is not a signal about its importance.

summaryParagraphs: State of the field, mid-2026: the "universal MLIP" era is now firmly post-hype. Foundation models (UMA, MACE-MP/OMAT, eSEN, GRACE, SevenNet, MatterSim) are commodities — Matbench Discovery lists 41 models, the top ~5 are separated by ~0.02 CPS, and MLIP Studio (arXiv:2607.07606) now serves 60+ of them from one web UI. That compression is the single most important strategic fact for a PhD student: architecture-chasing on energy/force MAE is a losing bet. The differentiating work has moved to (a) physics the short-range GNN ansatz structurally cannot represent — long-range electrostatics, charge transfer, spin, electronic entropy, excited states; (b) honesty about error — UQ that includes inherited DFT error, not just ensemble spread; and (c) whether any of it survives contact with a real simulation, where benchmarks are now exposing embarrassing gaps (pressure poorly described across most foundation models per Dyna-Mat arXiv:2607.03433; amorphous phases broken per Deringer arXiv:2607.11384; sophisticated models delivering 3-5 meV/atom for near-DFT wall-clock per arXiv:2607.07647).

Three asymmetries I'd flag for roadmap purposes. First, long-range electrostatics went from open problem to near-solved-in-principle in about 18 months — Kim & Cheng's "easier than we thought" (arXiv:2512.18029) argues latent Ewald bolts onto essentially any short-range MLIP, and MACE-POLAR-1 (arXiv:2602.19411, Batatia/Csányi, 100M hybrid-DFT structures) productionized it. The remaining open part is not "can we add Ewald" but "long-range still isn't enough": arXiv:2604.21222 shows long-range extensions still fail medium-range order in silica glass. Entering this now means entering late. Second, magnetism/spin and excited states are conspicuously underserved — the spin literature is a handful of groups (Shapeev's spin-MLIP, LANL's magnetic HIP-NN) and X-MACE is nearly alone on transferable excited-state surfaces. Third, and most underrated: efficiency and end-to-end observables are where the field's stated values and revealed values diverge most, and where a student can publish results the whole field needs but nobody is incentivized to produce.

On skills: the stack has consolidated hard around PyTorch + e3nn-style equivariance for models, and the interesting shift is that the simulation engine is being rewritten for GPUs (torch-sim, ~100x over ASE; GPUMD/NEP for million-atom). ASE remains the lingua franca but is increasingly the bottleneck, not the workhorse. Being fluent in fairchem + mace-torch + torch-sim + LAMMPS, and able to read i-PI for path-integral/nuclear-quantum work, covers ~90% of employable surface area. JAX-MD is alive (v0.2.29, June 2026) but is now a niche differentiable-simulation choice rather than a mainstream one.

Groups: Csányi (Cambridge) and Ceriotti (EPFL) dominate the physics-extension and UQ frontiers respectively; Deringer (Oxford) owns amorphous/disorder; Meta FAIR (fairchem/UMA, releasing on a ~quarterly cadence — core 2.21.0 as of June 2026) owns scale and data; Cheng (Berkeley) owns latent-Ewald electrostatics; Shapeev/Skoltech-lineage owns MTP+spin; Fan Zheyong's GPUMD/NEP community owns throughput and thermal transport.

Recommendation: pick a problem where the bottleneck is physics or evaluation, not parameters. The highest expected-value quadrants are (1) DFT-error inheritance + experimental anchoring, (2) spin/magnetism, (3) excited states, (4) rigorous end-to-end observable benchmarking. Avoid the architecture leaderboard and, at this point, avoid generic long-range electrostatics unless attacking the medium-range-order failure specifically.
